teile.einleitung: Plants have no skeleton, and yet they stand upright. Strengthening tissues take care of this. One of them is sclerenchyma, a tissue with especially hard cell walls.
wichtigste: Sclerenchyma is a strengthening tissue with thick, mostly lignified cell walls.
Mature sclerenchyma cells are often dead.
A distinction is made between long fibres and short sclereids, the stone cells.
Lignin makes the cell walls hard and resistant to compression.
Linen is made from the sclerenchyma fibres of flax.
Nutshells and cherry stones consist mainly of sclereids.

abschnitte.text: The word **sclerenchyma** comes from Greek and means roughly “hard tissue”. Its cells have greatly thickened walls. **Lignin** is usually deposited in these walls, which is called lignification. Lignin makes the wall hard, resistant to compression and hardly permeable. When mature, the cells are often dead, but they go on providing support.

There are two types of cell. **Sclerenchyma fibres** are long and spindle-shaped. They give stems tensile strength. **Sclereids** are rather short and rounded, and are also called **stone cells**. Both types have very thick walls.

When you eat a pear, you sometimes feel fine grains. These are groups of **stone cells** in the flesh. The hard shell of the walnut and the stone of the cherry consist of densely packed sclereids. The long bast fibres of **flax** are sclerenchyma fibres. **Linen** is made from them.

A second strengthening tissue is **collenchyma**. Its cells are alive and have unevenly thickened, unlignified walls. That is why it stays stretchy and can grow along. It therefore strengthens young, growing parts of plants. Sclerenchyma forms mainly in fully grown parts, because its rigid walls would hinder growth.

gewusst: The gritty spots in a pear are tiny stone cells.
Linen is among the oldest textile materials and comes from plant fibres that are sclerenchyma.

teile.einleitung: The sundew is a small plant that catches insects. It grows in bogs, where the soil has hardly any nutrients. Its leaves bear glistening, sticky drops that sparkle like dew in the sun.
wichtigste: The sundew is one of the carnivorous plants.
It grows in bogs with very nutrient-poor soil.
Sticky drops on red hairs hold insects fast.
The leaf slowly bends around the captured insect.
The round-leaved sundew has a rosette only a few centimetres across and white flowers.
In Switzerland the sundew is protected.

abschnitte.text: The **round-leaved sundew** is a small, inconspicuous plant. Its round leaves lie in a flat **rosette** only a few centimetres wide. On the leaves stand many **hairs**, which are mostly **red**. At their tips sit glistening drops. They sparkle in the sun like **dewdrops**, and that is where the plant gets its name.

The drops are not water but sticky like **glue**. If an insect lands on them, it stays stuck. Then the hairs and the leaf bend **slowly around the insect**. In this way the plant can digest it better. That is why the sundew is one of the **carnivorous plants**.

The sundew grows in **bogs**. In the wet bog soil there are hardly any **nutrients**. The captured insects supply it with extra nutrients. It does have green leaves, so it also makes its own food with sunlight.

In summer, small **white flowers** grow on a thin stalk. They stand far above the trapping leaves. In Switzerland the sundew is **protected**, and the bogs are protected too. You may not pick it, only look at it.

gewusst: The naturalist Charles Darwin studied the sundew closely and wrote a book about carnivorous plants.
In the green sphagnum moss, the red hairs of the sundew stand out at once.

teile.einleitung: Thyme is a small, fragrant herb found in many kitchens and gardens. It comes from the Mediterranean region and likes it sunny and dry. In Switzerland a wild relative also grows, wild thyme.
wichtigste: Common thyme comes from the Mediterranean region.
It has very small leaves and becomes woody with age.
Its flowers are mostly light purple to pink.
Thyme loves sunny, dry places.
The wild thyme in Switzerland is called “Quendel”.
Thyme tea is often drunk for coughs.

abschnitte.text: **Common thyme** is a low subshrub that grows about 10 to 40 centimetres tall. Its leaves are **very small**, narrow and often slightly rolled at the edge. Older stems become **woody**, and only the young shoots stay soft. In summer many small flowers appear, mostly **light purple to pink**. Thyme belongs to the **mint family**, like mint, sage and rosemary.

Common thyme originally grows on dry, stony slopes in the **Mediterranean region**. That is why in the garden, too, it likes a **sunny and dry** spot. Too much water and heavy, wet soil harm it. In Switzerland, **wild thyme** grows in the wild, also called creeping thyme. You find it on poor meadows, pastures and at the edges of paths, as high up as the Alps.

Thyme has a strong, spicy flavour. It goes well with **tomato sauce**, meat, potatoes and vegetables roasted in the oven. You can cook fresh sprigs along with the food and take them out later, or use dried leaves. There are many varieties, for example **lemon thyme**, which smells of lemon. Thyme is also part of the herb mixture “herbes de Provence”.

Thyme contains an **essential oil** with the substance **thymol**. This substance smells strong and stops bacteria from growing. That is why **thyme tea** has been drunk for a long time for **coughs** and colds. Pharmacies also sell cough syrup with thyme. For serious complaints, though, you should always see a doctor.

gewusst: The scent of thyme is held in tiny glandular hairs on the leaves.
Bees like to visit the flowers of thyme.

teile.einleitung: You find fir cones on every walk in the woods. The seeds of conifers lie between their scales. For squirrels and woodpeckers they are an important source of food.
wichtigste: The seeds lie between the scales of a cone.
When it rains the scales close, and in dry weather they open.
The seeds have a little wing and sail away on the wind.
Squirrels gnaw cones down to the core.
The great spotted woodpecker wedges cones into a woodpecker’s workshop.
Most conifers bear cones.

abschnitte.text: A cone consists of a central axis, the **spindle**, and many woody **scales**. The tree’s **seeds** lie between the scales. The cone protects them until they are ripe. Spruce, fir, pine, larch and Swiss stone pine all bear cones. Broadleaved trees, on the other hand, have other fruits such as nuts or berries.

Cones react to **moisture**. When it rains, the scales close so that the seeds stay dry. In dry weather they open again. This even works with cones that have been lying on the ground for a long time. Some people therefore use a cone as a simple **weather indicator**.

Many seeds in the cone have a thin **wing**. When they fall out, they spin and sail through the air. The **wind** carries them further away from the mother tree. That way new trees can grow in other places. Fresh cones are often sticky, because conifers produce **resin**, which protects the tree.

The **squirrel** bites off the scales to get at the seeds. What is left is a gnawed spindle with a few scales at the tip. The **great spotted woodpecker** wedges cones into a crack in the wood and hacks out the seeds. This workplace is called a **woodpecker’s workshop**. Underneath it you often find many shredded cones.

You can make bird food from cones. You press a mixture of **fat and seeds** between the scales. Then you hang the cone from a string in a tree. Tits and other birds like to peck at it in winter. Cones are also often used for Christmas decorations.

gewusst: The cones of the silver fir stand upright and fall apart while still on the tree, so most “fir cones” on the ground actually come from the spruce.
The cones of the Swiss stone pine do not open by themselves, and their seeds are spread mainly by the nutcracker.

teile.einleitung: A constellation is a group of stars in the night sky that you join in your mind into a picture. For thousands of years, people have seen animals, heroes and objects in them. Constellations still help us find our way around the sky today.
wichtigste: Constellations are groups of stars that are joined into pictures.
In 1922 the International Astronomical Union officially fixed 88 constellations.
Many names come from Greek myths.
The stars of a constellation are often at very different distances from us.
You see different constellations depending on the season.
The twelve constellations of the zodiac lie along the path of the Sun.

abschnitte.text: A constellation is a group of bright stars that seem to form a figure together. People joined the points with imaginary lines and recognised in them, for example, a hunter, a bear or a swan. Today every constellation is a precisely bounded field in the sky. In all, **88 constellations** divide the whole sky without any gaps.

The Babylonians and Egyptians already gave the stars names. The Greek scholar **Ptolemy** described 48 constellations in the 2nd century AD. Many names come from Greek legends, such as Orion, Perseus or Cassiopeia. The constellations of the southern sky were named by European seafarers only from the 16th century on.

The **Plough**, or Big Dipper, is really only a part of the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. Cassiopeia looks like a big W. In winter, **Orion** with its three belt stars is easy to find. In summer, the bright stars Vega, Deneb and Altair form the Summer Triangle.

abschnitte.titel: Finding your way in the sky
abschnitte.text: If you extend the two rear stars of the Plough about five times, you come to the **Pole Star**. It stands almost exactly above the North Pole and therefore shows the direction north. Seafarers used it for navigation in the past. Because the Earth circles the Sun, you see different constellations in every season.

Over the course of a year, the Sun seems to travel through a series of constellations. These are called the **zodiac**, and they include Aries, Taurus, Leo and Scorpio. Astronomy is a science, but astrology with its horoscopes is not. The stars of a constellation are often at different distances and in reality do not belong together.

Because of the many lights in cities, only a few stars can be seen there, which is called **light pollution**. In the mountains, for example in the Engadine or the Jura, the sky is much darker. In many places in Switzerland there are public observatories, for example the Urania in Zurich. There you may look through large telescopes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of stars that are joined into a picture.
A star that stands almost exactly in the north and shows the direction.
The twelve constellations through which the Sun seems to travel over the course of the year.
A building with telescopes for watching the sky.

gewusst: The largest constellation in the sky is Hydra, the water snake, and the smallest is the Southern Cross.
Over the course of the year the Sun also stands in the constellation Ophiuchus, which is not counted among the twelve signs of the zodiac.
The Southern Cross can never be seen from Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In summer, the water of a deep lake is not equally warm everywhere. At the top it is warm, in the depths cold. In between lies a layer in which the temperature drops sharply: the thermocline layer.
wichtigste: The thermocline layer of a lake is called the metalimnion in technical language.
It lies between the warm surface water and the cold deep water.
The zone of the steepest temperature drop is called the thermocline.
A drop of at least 1 °C per metre is often taken as the sign.
In summer, the thermocline layer prevents the lake from mixing.
In autumn it sinks and dissolves, and then the lake circulates.

abschnitte.text: In summer, the Sun warms the surface of a deep lake. Warm water is lighter than cold and stays on top. This produces a warm surface layer, the **epilimnion**. In the depths lies cold water, the **hypolimnion**. In between lies the **thermocline layer**, in technical language the **metalimnion**. Here the temperature falls sharply with depth.

The zone with the steepest temperature drop is called the **thermocline**. This term is used for lakes and oceans. A common definition requires a drop of **at least 1 °C per metre**. In deep lakes, this zone is often only a few metres thick. If it is not the temperature but the salt content that changes abruptly, it is called a **halocline**. In general, a layer with an abrupt change in water density is called a **pycnocline**.

Water of different **density** hardly mixes. The thermocline layer therefore acts like a **barrier**. In summer, hardly any oxygen from the air gets into the deep water. The oxygen there can only decrease during the summer. This matters for fish and other living things in the depths.

In autumn the surface cools. Cooling and **autumn storms** deepen the mixed layer. The thermocline layer sinks and **finally dissolves**. Then the whole lake can mix, and it is said to **circulate**. In this way oxygen reaches the depths again.

There are thermocline layers in the sea too. At the thermocline, **sound waves** are bent and deflected. A **submarine** below this layer is therefore harder to find with sonar. For shipping and marine research, the thermocline layer is therefore important.

gewusst: If you dive in a deep Swiss lake in summer, you can clearly feel the jump in temperature on your body.
Water is heaviest at about 4 °C, so the deep water of large lakes is often roughly at this temperature.

teile.einleitung: An allotment garden is a small garden that you rent in a garden complex. In Switzerland these are mostly called family gardens. Here city dwellers grow vegetables, fruit and flowers.
wichtigste: The German name for the allotment garden, “Schrebergarten”, comes from the Leipzig doctor Moritz Schreber.
In Switzerland allotment gardens are mostly called family gardens.
A single piece of garden is called a plot.
Usually an association rents out the plots.
Many garden rules require you to plant part of the area.
In the Second World War, Switzerland grew far more food with the Battle for Crops.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, cities grew strongly. Many **working-class families** lived in cramped flats without greenery. A small garden offered fresh air, exercise and extra **vegetables**. The Leipzig doctor **Moritz Schreber** campaigned for exercise in the fresh air. After his death, playgrounds and gardens in Leipzig were named after him.

In Switzerland people mostly speak of **family gardens**. They are often rented out by **associations** on land belonging to the **municipality**. A complex is divided into many **plots**. Each plot is rented by one person or family. In many cities there are waiting lists, because the gardens are very popular.

Anyone who rents a plot must keep to the **garden rules**. Family gardens are meant for **growing** things and not only for leisure. That is why many associations require part of the area to be used for vegetables, fruit or flowers. On many plots there is a **garden shed**. It serves as shelter and as storage for tools. Living in it is usually not allowed.

In the **Second World War**, Switzerland was surrounded by countries at war. It wanted to grow as much of its own food as possible. This plan was called the **Anbauschlacht**, or Battle for Crops. After its originator, **Friedrich Traugott Wahlen**, it is also called the **Wahlen Plan**. Even on sports fields and in parks, potatoes and vegetables grew. In many family gardens and allotments in the cities, too, vegetables were grown at that time.

gewusst: Friedrich Traugott Wahlen later became a Federal Councillor.
Family gardens are important green islands for birds and insects in the city.

teile.einleitung: The scythe is an old tool for mowing grass and grain. Before there were machines, almost all meadows were mown by hand with the scythe. In the mountains it is still used today.
wichtigste: A scythe is a tool for mowing.
Its blade is long and curved.
The long wooden handle is called the snath.
You hold the scythe with both hands on two grips.
While mowing, you sharpen the blade with a whetstone.
Beating the blade thin with a hammer is called peening.
Today the scythe is used mainly on steep slopes and at edges.

abschnitte.text: A scythe consists of a **long, curved blade** and a long handle made of wood, the **snath**. On the snath sit **two grips**. The blade is fixed almost at a right angle at the lower end. In many Swiss dialects the scythe is called **“Sägesse”**.

You hold the scythe **with both hands on the grips** and swing it in a flat arc from right to left just above the ground. In doing so the grass is cut off and laid to the side. Good mowing takes practice. The power comes mainly from a turn of the upper body, not only from the arms. It is best to mow early in the morning, when the grass is still damp with dew.

A scythe must be very sharp. During the work you sharpen the blade again and again with a **whetstone**. You carry this in a small container filled with water at your belt so that it stays damp. From time to time the cutting edge also has to be **peened**. In this you beat it **thin** with a hammer on a small anvil. In this way it becomes fine and sharp again.

Today machines mostly do the mowing. The scythe is still used, however, where machines cannot go: on **steep slopes**, at the edges of paths, on stream banks and around trees. Especially in the Swiss **mountains**, some farming families still mow steep meadows by hand. Mowing with a scythe also spares insects and other small animals in the meadow.

Related to the scythe is the **sickle**. It has a **short, strongly curved blade** and only a small handle. You hold it in one hand and use it to cut smaller amounts of grass or grain. The sickle is even older than the scythe.

gewusst: In some regions there are scything competitions.
For a long time the scythe was the most important tool for the hay harvest, with which farmers collected fodder for the winter.

teile.einleitung: The pansy is a cheerful, colourful flower that you often see on balconies and in gardens. Many of the flowers look as if they had a little face.
wichtigste: Pansies are often planted on the balcony in spring.
Many flowers have a marking like a little face.
They grow to about a hand’s height.
A flower has 5 petals.
Pansies belong to the violets.
Their flowers can be eaten and used to decorate salad.

abschnitte.text: The flowers of the pansy come in **many bright colours**: violet, yellow, white, blue, orange and almost black. Often they have dark blotches and lines in the middle. In this way the flower looks like a **little face**. Each flower has **5 petals**. The plant grows to about **a hand’s height**.

The pansy belongs to the **violets**. Like the sweet violet, it has flowers with a small spur at the back. The garden pansy was bred by gardeners. Its small wild sister is called the **wild pansy**. It has smaller flowers, mostly in violet, yellow and white, and grows in meadows and fields.

In German the pansy is called a “little stepmother”, and there is an old explanation for this name. The lowest, largest petal is the **stepmother**. The two petals beside it are her own daughters, nicely dressed. The two upper petals are the **stepdaughters**, who get only a plain dress. This is of course only a story, but one that is easy to remember.

abschnitte.titel: In the garden and in the kitchen
abschnitte.text: Pansies tolerate cold well. That is why they are often planted on the balcony as early as **spring**, some also in autumn. They like a bright spot and regular water. You pinch off faded flowers, and then new ones come. The flowers are edible. You can use them to **decorate a salad** or trim a cake.

gewusst: The wild pansy is called “Viola tricolor” in Latin, which means “three-coloured violet”.
Pansies sometimes even bloom while snow still lies on the ground.

teile.einleitung: Hoverflies look like small wasps but are harmless flies. They can stay in one spot in the air and are important helpers in the garden.
wichtigste: Hoverflies belong to the flies and have two wings.
Many resemble wasps but can never sting.
The stripes protect them, because enemies take them for wasps.
They can stay in one spot in the air.
Adult hoverflies eat nectar and pollen.
The larvae of many species eat aphids.

abschnitte.text: Hoverflies belong to the **flies**. Like all flies, they have only **two wings**, while wasps and bees have four. Many hoverflies wear yellow and black stripes. You recognise them by their short antennae and the large eyes that cover almost the whole head. There are several thousand species worldwide.

Hoverflies have no sting and can **never sting**. Their stripes are a kind of camouflage. Birds and other enemies have learned that wasps sting, and avoid striped insects. The harmless hoverflies benefit from this. This imitation of a well-defended animal is called **mimicry**.

Hoverflies are excellent fliers. With very fast wing beats they can **hang in one spot in the air**, almost like a helicopter. That is where they get their name. In a flash they then shoot to the side or forwards. You often see them hovering over flowers.

Adult hoverflies feed on **nectar and pollen**. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower. In this way they help to pollinate plants, similar to bees. They especially like to visit open, flat flowers where they can easily reach the food.

The females often lay their eggs near colonies of aphids. The **larvae** of many species look like small maggots and eat **aphids**, one after another. A single larva can devour a great many aphids during its development. That is why hoverflies are popular with gardeners as **beneficial insects**.

gewusst: The larva of the drone fly, a kind of hoverfly, lives in muddy water and breathes through a long breathing tube. It is therefore called the rat-tailed maggot.
Some hoverflies migrate like migratory birds and fly south in large numbers over the Alpine passes in autumn.

teile.einleitung: The pea family is a large group of plants that includes pea, bean, clover and lentil. Their flowers recall a butterfly. With the help of bacteria, they can use nitrogen from the air.
wichtigste: A pea-family flower consists of a standard, wings and a keel.
Plants of the pea family form pods as fruits.
Nodule bacteria in the roots fix nitrogen from the air.
The peanut is botanically a legume.
Tofu is made from soya beans.
Laburnum is highly poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The flower of a **pea-family plant** has a special structure. At the top stands the large **standard**. At the sides lie two **wings**. Below, two fused petals form the **keel**. The stamens lie hidden inside it. When bees and bumblebees land, they press the keel down and so reach the pollen.

Plants of the pea family form a **pod** as their fruit. It develops from a single carpel and opens along two seams. That is why beans, peas and **lentils** are also called **pulses**. Lentils come in red, yellow, green and black varieties. Red lentils fall apart quickly when cooked and are often used for the Indian **dal**.

In the roots of many plants of the pea family live **nodule bacteria**. They fix **nitrogen** from the air and give it to the plant. In return they receive sugar. That is why **clover** and **lucerne** fertilise the soil in a natural way. **Red clover**, with its three-part leaves, is a protein-rich animal feed, also on Swiss meadows.

The **peanut** is not a true nut but a member of the pea family. After flowering, its fruit stalk grows into the ground, where the pods ripen. The **soya bean** is very rich in protein. Soya milk is made from soaked soya beans. If it is made to curdle and pressed, **tofu** is the result.

Not all plants of the pea family are edible. **Laburnum** is an ornamental shrub with long, hanging yellow flower clusters. All its parts, especially the seeds, contain the poison **cytisine**. Children should never put them in their mouths. The **black locust** from North America has feathered leaves and thorns. It was introduced as an ornamental tree and is regarded in Switzerland today as an **invasive neophyte**.

gewusst: The black locust is often called the false acacia.
Farmers sow clover to supply the soil with nitrogen without artificial fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: The stamen is the part of the flower that makes pollen. Without stamens there would be no pollination, and so no seeds and fruit either.
wichtigste: A stamen consists of the filament and the anther.
Pollen is made in the anther.
Pollen is sometimes also called flower dust.
A hermaphrodite flower has stamens and carpels at the same time.
A male flower has only stamens.
In double flowers, many stamens have turned into petals.

abschnitte.text: A stamen has two parts. At the bottom is the **filament**, a thin stalk. At the top sits the **anther**, in which the pollen is made. When the pollen is ripe, the anther opens and releases the fine grains. That is why pollen is also called **flower dust**. The number of stamens is typical in many plants: the white dead-nettle, for example, has exactly **4**.

For a plant to make seeds, pollen has to reach the stigma of a flower. This process is called **pollination**. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies brush off the pollen while collecting nectar and carry it on. In grasses and many trees, the **wind** does this job. Wind-pollinated plants therefore make huge amounts of pollen, which gives some people hay fever.

Many flowers have stamens and carpels at the same time. They are called **hermaphrodite flowers**, and one example is the cherry blossom. If a flower has only stamens, it is called a **male flower**. The hazel bears male and female flowers separately, but on the same shrub. Such plants are called **monoecious**. The long hazel catkins in early spring are the male flowers.

In many garden roses you hardly see any stamens, but very many petals. Here stamens have turned into additional **petals**. Such flowers are called **double flowers**. They are magnificent, but often offer insects little pollen and nectar. Anyone who wants to help bees therefore prefers to plant single flowers.

gewusst: The yellow clouds that lie over spruce forests in spring consist of pollen.
Under the microscope, every plant species has its own pollen shape.

teile.einleitung: A stereo microscope is a microscope with which you can see small things in three dimensions and magnified. In Swiss schools it is often simply called a binocular microscope.
wichtigste: In a stereo microscope, each eye has its own light path.
That is why you see a three-dimensional image.
Usually the object is lit from above with reflected light.
You do not need a wafer-thin section, and whole objects fit underneath.
It magnifies much less than a light microscope for cells.
The image appears upright and the right way round.

abschnitte.text: Our two eyes always see a thing from slightly different angles. The brain puts the two images together into a **three-dimensional image**. The stereo microscope does exactly the same: **each eye has its own light path**. So you see two slightly different images. In this way an insect or a flower does not look flat but three-dimensional.

In an ordinary light microscope, the light shines from below through a thin specimen. In a stereo microscope, you mostly use **reflected light from above**. The light is thrown back by the object. That is why you need **no wafer-thin section**. You can put a **whole small flower**, a beetle, a stone or a coin straight under the instrument.

A stereo microscope magnifies **much less** than a light microscope. Usually it is about 10 to 40 times. Individual cells can hardly be seen with it. But it is suitable for things that you cannot see well enough with a magnifying glass. The image appears **upright and the right way round**: what lies on the left, you also see on the left. In a light microscope, by contrast, the image is often reversed.

Between the objective and the object there is a lot of room. This **working distance** is used to work with **tweezers** and a needle. In this way you can, for example, carefully take a flower apart. Watchmakers, dental technicians and medical specialists also work with similar instruments. At school, the **binocular microscope** is ideal for exploring plants and small animals.

gewusst: The word “binocular” means “with both eyes”.
Under the stereo microscope you can see the fine scales on a butterfly’s wing.

teile.einleitung: Butterflies are insects with large, often colourful wings that drink nectar from flowers with a long proboscis. Before they can fly, they live as a caterpillar and transform in a pupa. This transformation is one of the most exciting wonders of nature.
wichtigste: Butterflies are insects with six legs and four wings.
Their wings are covered with tiny scales.
They suck nectar from flowers with a coiled proboscis.
They go through a complete metamorphosis: egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult.
There are far more than 150,000 species, most of them moths.
Butterflies pollinate flowers and are food for many animals.
Many species are threatened in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Butterflies, also called **lepidopterans**, have six legs like all insects and a body made up of head, thorax and abdomen. Their four wings are covered with thousands of tiny **scales** that lie one over another like roof tiles. These scales produce the colours and patterns. On the head they have two antennae and a long **proboscis**, which they coil up like a garden hose.

The female lays her eggs on a suitable food plant. From them hatches a **caterpillar**, which does almost nothing but eat and moults several times. Then it transforms into a **pupa**, which in day-flying butterflies is often called a chrysalis. In the pupa the body is completely rebuilt until a finished butterfly hatches.

Adult butterflies mainly drink sweet **nectar** from flowers. Some also suck at rotting fruit, tree sap or damp ground to take in salts. Caterpillars, by contrast, eat leaves, and many species depend on one particular plant. The caterpillars of the peacock butterfly, for example, eat almost only stinging nettles.

Far more than 150,000 species of butterflies and moths are known worldwide. Most are **moths**, which are seen less often than the colourful day-flying butterflies. In Switzerland about 3,700 species live, of which about 200 are day-flying butterflies. Well-known examples are the brimstone, the swallowtail and the small tortoiseshell.

Butterflies **pollinate** flowers and are food for birds, bats and spiders. Unfortunately their numbers are falling because flower meadows are disappearing and poisons are being used. Almost half of the day-flying butterflies in Switzerland are on the **Red List** of threatened species. Anyone who has a natural garden with wild flowers and a few nettles is helping the butterflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a butterfly or moth.
The larva of the butterfly, which mainly eats and grows.
The resting stage in which the caterpillar rebuilds itself into a butterfly.
The complete transformation from caterpillar to butterfly.

gewusst: Butterflies taste with their feet.
The monarch butterfly migrates thousands of kilometres every year from Canada to Mexico.
In spring the painted lady flies from North Africa over the Alps as far as Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A supernova is the gigantic explosion of a massive star at the end of its life. For a short time, it can shine brighter than a whole galaxy with billions of stars. In the process, many chemical elements are made, from which new stars, planets and even people later form.
wichtigste: A supernova is the explosion of a star.
Massive stars explode when their fuel is used up.
White dwarfs can also explode when they suck in matter from a neighbouring star.
A supernova can shine brighter than a whole galaxy.
What is left behind is a neutron star or a black hole.
Supernovae spread heavy elements such as iron through space.

abschnitte.text: A supernova is the explosive end of a star. The name comes from Latin, nova meaning new, because in the past people believed a new star had appeared. Within a few days, the star becomes billions of times brighter. Then it fades again over weeks and months.

Stars with at least about eight solar masses burn ever heavier elements in their interior, right up to **iron**. No more energy can be gained from iron. Then the core collapses under its own weight in fractions of a second, which is called **core collapse**. The outer layers bounce off and are hurled into space with enormous force.

There is a second kind of supernova. A **white dwarf**, the remnant of a smaller star, sucks gas from a neighbouring star. If it becomes too heavy, a thermonuclear explosion ignites in it that tears it apart completely. Because these explosions are always similarly bright, astronomers use them to measure distances in space.

After a core-collapse supernova, an extremely dense **neutron star** remains. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth. If the remnant is especially heavy, a black hole forms. The gases that were hurled away form a glowing **supernova remnant**, for example the Crab Nebula.

In the year 1054, Chinese astronomers observed a new star that could even be seen in daytime. Its remnant is today’s **Crab Nebula** in the constellation Taurus. In 1572 Tycho Brahe described a supernova, and in 1604 Johannes Kepler did too. Supernova 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud was the brightest for almost 400 years.

In supernovae, many **heavy elements** such as iron, calcium and gold are made and spread through space. From this dust, new stars and planets later formed, including our Earth. The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were once made in stars. That is why astronomers like to say that we are made of stardust.

begriffe.erklaerung: The gigantic explosion of a star.
A tiny, extremely dense stellar remnant after a supernova.
The small, hot remnant of a star like the Sun.
The mass of the Sun, used as a yardstick for other stars.

gewusst: In our Milky Way, it is estimated that a star explodes as a supernova only about once to three times per century.
The star Betelgeuse in Orion will one day explode as a supernova, which is harmless for the Earth.
The Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky coined the term supernova in the 1930s together with Walter Baade.

teile.einleitung: Many plants protect themselves from hungry animals with sharp parts. In everyday speech these are often called thorns. In botany, however, a precise distinction is made between prickles and thorns. The rose, for example, actually has prickles.
wichtigste: Prickles grow only from the outer skin and bark of the plant.
That is why prickles can easily be broken off the twig.
Thorns are firmly joined to the wood and are modified plant parts.
The rose has prickles, not thorns.
The blackberry also bears prickles on its shoots.
The gooseberry gets its name from its prickles.

abschnitte.text: A **prickle** grows only from the outer skin and the **bark** of the plant. It sits, so to speak, on the outside. That is why it can be **broken off easily**. A **thorn**, by contrast, is a modified plant part, for example a leaf or a short twig. It is firmly joined to the **wood** and does not break off so easily.

In everyday speech people often say that roses have thorns. Botanically that is not correct. The sharp parts of the **rose** are **prickles**. They sit only on the outside of the bark. If you press against them from the side, they come away from the twig easily.

The **blackberry** also has prickles. Its long shoots are densely covered with them. That is why you need care and long sleeves when picking. The **gooseberry** even carries the prickles in its name. It has sharp prickles on its twigs.

Prickles protect the plant from **animals** that want to eat leaves and shoots. In climbing plants such as the blackberry, they also help with **holding on**. The backward-curved prickles hook into other plants. In this way the plant can grow far upwards and sideways.

gewusst: True thorns are found, for example, on the hawthorn, where short twigs are modified into sharp points.
The sharp parts of many cacti are modified leaves and are therefore botanically thorns.

teile.einleitung: Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site in the Bernese Alps. Here lies the Great Aletsch Glacier, the longest glacier in the Alps. The area stretches from the canton of Bern to the Valais.
wichtigste: Since 2001 the area has been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site.
It was the first World Natural Heritage site in the Alps.
The World Heritage site lies in the cantons of Bern and Valais.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is about 20 kilometres long.
Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau stand on the northern edge.
Because of global warming, the glacier is getting shorter and thinner.

abschnitte.text: UNESCO added the area in 2001 to the list of **World Natural Heritage**. It was the first World Natural Heritage site in the whole of the Alps. At first it was called **Jungfrau-Aletsch-Bietschhorn**, after three well-known names of the region. In 2007 the area was enlarged. Today it is called Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch and lies in the cantons of **Bern** and **Valais**.

The **Great Aletsch Glacier** is about 20 kilometres long and the largest glacier in the Alps. It begins at the **Konkordiaplatz**, where several ice streams flow together. There the ice is several hundred metres thick. From there the glacier flows slowly towards the Rhone valley. For decades it has been getting shorter and thinner because of **global warming**, since more ice melts in summer than is added in winter.

On the northern edge of the World Heritage site stand the **Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau**. This trio can be seen from the Bernese Oberland and, in clear weather, even from the Central Plateau. Many other four-thousanders and glaciers belong to the area. The landscape shows very beautifully how ice shapes valleys. Researchers observe here how glaciers and plant life are changing.

Above the glacier lies the **Aletsch Forest**. Here very old **Swiss stone pines** grow, some of them several hundred years old. Stone pines withstand great cold and grow close to the treeline. The Aletsch Forest is a nature reserve of **Pro Natura**. On hiking trails you can see marmots, chamois and many mountain flowers.

gewusst: At the Konkordiaplatz, the ice of the Aletsch Glacier is thicker than most tall buildings are high.
The north side of the World Heritage site belongs to the canton of Bern, the south side with the Aletsch Glacier to the Valais.

teile.einleitung: The true grasses are a huge plant family. They include the grasses of meadow and lawn, but also cereals such as wheat, rice and maize, and even bamboo. Without true grasses, people and many animals would have hardly anything to eat.
wichtigste: The stem of a grass is called a culm and is mostly hollow inside.
The thickened places on the culm are called nodes.
Cereals such as wheat, rice and maize are true grasses.
Bamboo is also a true grass.
The pollen of grasses often triggers hay fever.
Buckwheat, despite its name, is not a true grass.

abschnitte.text: The stem of a grass is called a **culm**. It is mostly hollow inside and yet very stable. Thickened places, the **nodes**, divide it into sections. From each node grows a long, narrow leaf. Grass is green because of the **chlorophyll**, with which it makes food from sunlight.

The most important food plants in the world are true grasses. They include **wheat**, barley, rye, oats, **rice** and **maize**. Bread is baked from wheat, and **polenta** is cooked from maize grains. Rice often grows in Asia in fields that stand under water. Sugar cane is also a true grass.

**Bamboo** is a woody true grass. Some species grow as tall as trees. Some are among the fastest growing plants in the world. Giant pandas eat almost only bamboo. In Asia, bamboo is even used to build scaffolding and houses.

Grasses have inconspicuous flowers without coloured petals. The **wind** carries their flower dust, the **pollen**, from plant to plant. Many people react to it with an allergy, which is called **hay fever**. The nose runs and the eyes itch. In Switzerland, the grass pollen season is mainly in early summer.

abschnitte.titel: Lawn, meadow and a false friend
abschnitte.text: A **lawn** is a grass area that is often mown. Grasses grow back quickly after mowing, because their growth begins close to the ground. That is also why they stand up well to being grazed by cows. **Buckwheat**, by contrast, is not a true grass but a member of the knotweed family. Its grains are used in a similar way to cereals, for example for pizzoccheri.

gewusst: There are around 12,000 species of true grass.
Rice, wheat and maize together provide a large part of the food of all people.

teile.einleitung: The soya bean is one of the most important crop plants in the world. From it people make tofu, soy sauce, oil and animal feed. It comes from East Asia and is grown today on all continents.
wichtigste: The soya bean is a legume, related to pea, lentil and bean.
It was bred from a wild plant in China thousands of years ago.
Dried soya beans consist of about a third protein.
In 2023, Brazil and the USA harvested the most soya beans.
After palm oil, soya oil is the vegetable oil produced in the greatest quantity.
Miso, tofu and edamame are well-known foods made from soya.

abschnitte.text: The soya bean belongs to the **legumes**. It forms hairy pods with usually two to three seeds. It was bred thousands of years ago in **China** from a wild plant. From **East Asia** it spread all over the world. Like other legumes, it lives together with bacteria in its roots that fix nitrogen from the air.

Dried soya beans consist of about a third **protein**. This makes them among the plants richest in protein of all. For people who eat vegetarian or vegan, soya is therefore valuable. From soya milk, for example, **tofu** is made.

In Japan, **miso** is popular, a seasoning paste made from fermented soya beans. It matures for months with salt and a noble mould, koji. Miso soup is cooked from it. **Edamame** are young, green soya beans that are boiled in the pod and lightly salted. **Soy sauce** is also made from fermented soya beans.

In 2023, **Brazil** and the **USA** together harvested well over half of all soya beans. China is the biggest buyer. Pressing produces **soya oil**, after palm oil the vegetable oil produced in the greatest quantity. The rest, the soya meal, is largely fed to farm animals. For new growing areas, forests in South America have also been cleared, which is often criticised.

gewusst: The largest part of the world’s soya harvest ends up not on our plates but in animal feed.
The word “edamame” comes from Japanese.

teile.einleitung: The white willow is the largest native willow. It grows by rivers and streams and is also called the silver willow because of its silvery shining leaves. It has been important to people and animals for a long time.
wichtigste: The white willow is also called the silver willow because its leaves shine silvery.
It grows by rivers and streams.
It is the largest native willow.
It withstands flooding especially well.
Pollarded willows arise when the branches at the top of the trunk are cut off again and again.
In the past, willow bark was used against fever and pain.
In spring, willow flowers are an important first food for bees.

abschnitte.text: As the **largest native willow**, the white willow grows into a stately tree over 20 metres tall. Its leaves are long and narrow. Especially on the underside they are covered with fine, silky hairs. In the wind they therefore **shine silvery**. That is where its name comes from. The scientific name is Salix alba, and “alba” means white.

In the wild, the white willow grows **by rivers and streams**, in damp **floodplain forests** and on lake shores. It withstands **flooding** especially well and can stand in water for weeks. Its roots hold the bank firm. Broken-off twigs can even put down new roots in damp soil and become new trees.

In the past, the branches of many willows were cut off again and again at the top of the trunk. This created **pollarded willows** with a thick “head” from which new rods grow every year. From the **flexible willow rods**, **baskets**, fences and other objects were woven. In the hollows of old pollarded willows, birds such as the little owl often nest.

Willow bark was used long ago as a home remedy **against fever and pain**. It contains the substance **salicin**. From it, chemists later developed similar substances that are used as medicines. Well known is acetylsalicylic acid, the active ingredient of aspirin.

In spring, willows form fluffy flower clusters, the **catkins**. They bloom very early, when little else is blooming. For **bees**, bumblebees and other insects they are therefore an important **first food** with plenty of pollen and nectar. The seeds later bear white hairs and fly away with the wind.

gewusst: A cut willow twig that you stick in damp soil often simply takes root.
The name of the active substance salicin comes from the Latin name of the willow, Salix.

teile.einleitung: The tobacco mosaic virus infects tobacco and many other plants. It was the first virus that researchers discovered. With it began virology, the science of viruses.
wichtigste: The tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus to be discovered.
Dmitri Ivanovsky showed in 1892 that the pathogen passes through bacterial filters.
Martinus Beijerinck called it a “contagium vivum fluidum” in 1898.
The virus is rod-shaped and has single-stranded RNA.
Wendell Stanley crystallised it in 1935.
The virus is transmitted mechanically through hands, tools and plant sap.

abschnitte.text: Infected plants get leaves with pale and dark patches. The pattern looks like a **mosaic**, which is why the disease has this name. The plants grow less well and give a smaller yield. The virus infects not only tobacco but also other plants such as tomatoes. It is very stable and gets into the plant through small **wounds**.

The Russian researcher **Dmitri Ivanovsky** filtered the sap of sick tobacco plants through porcelain filters in 1892. These filters hold back bacteria. But the sap stayed **infectious**. The Dutchman **Martinus Beijerinck** concluded in 1898 that there was a living, liquid infectious agent. He called it a “contagium vivum fluidum” and is regarded as one of the founders of **virology**.

**Wendell Stanley** managed in 1935 to crystallise the virus. In this way he showed that a virus can behave like a chemical substance. For this he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in 1946. Later, **Rosalind Franklin** used X-ray diffraction to study how the RNA lies inside the virus. Her work helped greatly in understanding the structures of viruses.

The virus is a rigid **rod**. Inside lies a single strand of **RNA**, that is, genetic material. Around it, many identical **coat proteins** arrange themselves in a spiral. In the 1950s, **Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat** and **Robley Williams** separated RNA and coat protein and mixed them again. The parts put themselves together into infectious viruses, which is called **self-assembly**.

gewusst: Tobacco products can also contain infectious tobacco mosaic viruses, which is why washing hands is important in gardening.
Because it is so simply built, the tobacco mosaic virus is among the best researched viruses of all.

teile.einleitung: The yellow flag iris is also called the yellow iris. It grows at ponds, streams and in marshes and shines in early summer with large yellow flowers. Its long, pointed leaves gave it its German name, which means swamp sword lily.
wichtigste: The yellow flag iris blooms bright yellow.
Its leaves are long, flat and pointed like a sword.
It grows on the bank and in shallow water.
It blooms from about May to July.
All parts of the plant are poisonous.
It belongs to the genus Iris.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of the yellow flag iris are long, flat and taper to a point. They recall a **sword blade**, which is where the plant gets its German name. The plant often grows a metre tall or a little higher. Under the ground it has a thick **rhizome**. From it new leaves and flower stalks grow every year.

The flower is bright **yellow** and appears from about May to July. It has three large petals that hang outwards. Between them stand smaller, upright petals. On the hanging petals you often see fine brown lines. They show insects such as bumblebees the way to the nectar.

The yellow flag iris loves wet feet. It grows at **ponds**, streams, ditches and in marshes, often even in shallow water. Its dense stands offer frogs, dragonflies and insects hiding places. It is also happily planted in garden ponds. Its seeds can **float** and drift with the water to new places.

The irises form the genus **Iris**. The name comes from the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because irises come in very many colours. Many species of iris grow as ornamental plants in gardens. The yellow flag iris, however, is **poisonous**, especially its rhizome. You must not eat any part of it.

gewusst: The seeds of the yellow flag iris contain a layer of air and therefore stay on the water surface for a long time.
Although it is called a lily in German, the iris does not belong to the lily family but to the iris family.

teile.einleitung: The Sihlwald in the canton of Zurich is one of the largest continuous beech forests on the Swiss Central Plateau. Since about 2000, no timber has been harvested there, so that the forest can develop back into wilderness.
wichtigste: The Sihlwald lies in the canton of Zurich in the Sihl valley.
It is shaped mainly by the common beech.
Since about 2000, the city of Zurich has given up harvesting timber.
In the west the Sihlwald is bounded by the range of hills of the Albis.
In the past the timber was floated down the Sihl to the city.
Together with the Langenberg Wildlife Park it forms the Wildnispark Zürich.
The Sihl Valley Railway has a station right at the Sihlwald.

abschnitte.text: The Sihlwald lies in the **canton of Zurich** in the valley of the Sihl, south of the city of Zurich. On the west side it is bounded by the range of hills of the **Albis**. The forest is shaped mainly by the **common beech**. For centuries it has belonged to the **city of Zurich**.

Over many centuries the Sihlwald supplied timber for Zurich, for building and for heating. The timber was **floated** down the **Sihl** to the city. That is, the trunks were left to drift down the river. Later roads and the railway were added. The **Sihl Valley Railway** now runs through the Sihl valley and has a station right at the Sihlwald.

Since about **2000**, the city of Zurich has given up harvesting timber in the Sihlwald. The forest is to develop naturally again. Trees may grow old, fall over and stay lying. In the long term, **more old trees** and **more dead wood** are therefore expected. Dead wood is very valuable, because fungi, beetles and many other living things live in it.

Together with the **Langenberg Wildlife Park** near Langnau am Albis, the Sihlwald forms the **Wildnispark Zürich**. In the Langenberg live animals that were once native to Switzerland or still are, such as deer, wild boar, wolves, bears and elk. In the Sihlwald you can discover wild nature along paths. A visitor centre explains the forest.

gewusst: As a “Nature Experience Park”, the Wildnispark Zürich Sihlwald is a Park of National Importance in Switzerland.
Because the Sihlwald is no longer tidied up, forest scenes are appearing again like those in primeval forests.

teile.einleitung: Ferns, mosses and many fungi do not form seeds but spores. These arise in small containers, the sporangia. Under a fern frond you can often see them as brown clusters.
wichtigste: A sporangium is a container in which spores arise.
In ferns, many sporangia together form a cluster, the sorus.
In many ferns, a thin membrane, the indusium, protects the sori.
The ring of cells, the annulus, tears the ripe capsule open and flings the spores away.
A fern sporangium usually produces 64 spores.
A leaf that bears sporangia is called a sporophyll.

abschnitte.text: A **sporangium** is a small capsule in which **spores** are formed. When the capsule is ripe, it opens and releases the spores. A leaf that bears sporangia is called a **sporophyll**. In some ferns these leaves look quite different from the other fronds.

In many ferns the sporangia stand together in groups. Such a group is called a **sorus**, plural **sori**. You see them as dots or lines on the underside of the fronds. In many ferns a thin membrane protects the sori, the **indusium**. In the male fern, for example, it is kidney-shaped.

On a fern sporangium sits a ring of specially built cells, the **annulus**. As it dries out, it tenses. Then it tears the capsule open and flings the spores away. In this way they get into the air and are spread by the wind.

In a fern sporangium there are usually **16 spore mother cells**. Each divides into **4 spores**, which makes **64 spores** together. This division is called **meiosis**. In it, the number of chromosomes is halved.

Ferns are not the only ones with sporangia. In the **horsetail**, they sit on small, shield-shaped scales. These stand densely in a **cone-like spike** at the tip of the shoot. Mosses, too, form their spores in a capsule on a little stalk.

gewusst: With a magnifying glass you can see the tiny sporangia well under a ripe fern frond.
The annulus acts like a spring that tenses as it dries and suddenly snaps loose.

t1cxuns9.t: Test plantings of tree species for the future

teile.einleitung: Climate change is altering the conditions for Swiss forests. In the project “Test plantings of tree species for the future”, researchers are checking which trees can cope with the future climate. To do this, they plant different tree species at many places in Switzerland and observe them over a long time.
wichtigste: The main partners are the research institute WSL and the Federal Office for the Environment FOEN.
Cantonal forestry services and forest owners also take part.
The test sites are spread across the whole of Switzerland.
Native and foreign species are tested, for example Douglas fir, Atlas cedar and sweet chestnut.
Growth, survival and damage are recorded.
The trials last for decades, because trees live a very long time.

abschnitte.text: The project is run by the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research **WSL** and the Federal Office for the Environment **FOEN**. They work together with **cantonal forestry services** and forest owners. Together they test which tree species can cope with the future climate. The results should help foresters to plant the right trees. After all, a tree planted today still has to be healthy in many decades.

The test plantings are at many **sites** across Switzerland. They are spread over different altitudes, regions and soils. Some places already have a climate today that will only be found elsewhere in the future. That makes it possible to compare tree species under very **different conditions**. From this, it can be estimated which species can survive where.

Native and foreign tree species are tested. The **Douglas fir** comes from the west of North America and was brought to Europe in the 19th century. It grows quickly and is considered more tolerant of drought than the spruce. The **Atlas cedar** grows naturally in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco and Algeria. The **sweet chestnut** has shaped the south side of the Alps since Roman times and could become more important in the Central Plateau too if the climate gets warmer.

The researchers do not only measure how fast the trees grow. They also record exactly how many **survive**. Damage caused by **drought**, **late frost** and **pests** is important. A tree for the future has to endure heat and still survive cold nights in spring. Because trees often stand in the same place for over 100 years, trials like this last **decades**.

abschnitte.titel: Not all eggs in one basket
abschnitte.text: Behind the project is the principle of **spreading the risk**. If one tree species fails because of drought or pests, other species can keep the forest going. **Mixed forests** are therefore considered more resilient. This matters because the Swiss forest also protects against avalanches and rockfall. Nobody knows exactly what the climate will be like in 100 years.

gewusst: A test tree planted today may only give a finished result for the grandchildren of today’s researchers.
The sweet chestnut was probably encouraged by the Romans on the south side of the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Stomata are tiny pores, mostly on the underside of leaves. Through them the plant exchanges gases such as CO2 and oxygen with the air. At the same time, it can use them to control how much water it loses.
wichtigste: Stomata, also called stomatal pores, are tiny pores in the leaf surface.
They serve for the exchange of gases such as CO2 and oxygen.
Each stoma is formed by two bean-shaped guard cells.
The plant can open and close its stomata.
Water also evaporates through the stomata.
In drought, plants close their stomata in order to save water.

abschnitte.text: A stoma is a tiny opening in the skin of a leaf, the **epidermis**. It is so small that you can only see it under the **microscope**. The plural is **stomata**. On a single square millimetre of leaf there can, depending on the plant, be dozens to hundreds of them.

Each stoma is framed by two **guard cells** that look like two beans. Between them lies a narrow gap. When the guard cells fill with water, they curve and the gap opens. When they lose water, they go limp and the gap closes.

For **photosynthesis**, the plant needs carbon dioxide from the air. This gas streams through the stomata into the leaf. The oxygen that is produced streams out by the same route. At night, when no photosynthesis takes place, the stomata of many plants are closed.

Water constantly evaporates through the open stomata, which is called **transpiration**. This evaporation pulls water from the roots up into the leaves, rather as with a drinking straw. It also cools the leaves on hot days. A large deciduous tree can evaporate several hundred litres of water on a summer day.

In drought, plants close their stomata so that they do not die of thirst. In most plants they lie on the shady underside of the leaf, where less water evaporates. Water lilies, by contrast, have their stomata on the upper side, because the underside lies on the water. Cacti open them only at night, when it is cooler, and store the CO2 until the morning.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical word for a pore in the leaf surface, plural stomata.
One of the two cells that open and close the stoma.
The evaporation of water through the leaves.
How plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen from CO2 and water.

gewusst: The name stoma comes from Greek and means mouth.
From the stomata of old leaves, researchers can read off how much CO2 there used to be in the air.
Over 90 per cent of the water that a plant takes up evaporates again through its leaves.

teile.einleitung: The edible morel is one of the first edible mushrooms of the year. It appears in spring and has a cap that looks like a honeycomb. Mushroom gatherers prize it highly, but you must know it well and prepare it correctly.
wichtigste: The cap of the edible morel is honeycomb-like, with ridges and deep pits.
Morels grow in spring, mostly between March and May.
Raw, morels are poisonous, and you must cook them thoroughly.
Cut open lengthways, the edible morel is completely hollow inside.
It can be confused with the poisonous false morel.
Morels belong to the sac fungi.

abschnitte.text: The cap of the **edible morel** is covered with ridges and deep **pits**. It recalls a **honeycomb** or a sponge. If you cut the mushroom open lengthways, you see that cap and stem together form a single **hollow space**. This feature helps to tell the morel from look-alikes.

Morels usually appear between **March and May**. This makes them among the first edible mushrooms of the year. In Switzerland you often find them in floodplain forests, at woodland edges and under **ash trees**. They also often turn up on burnt ground. Because they are well camouflaged, you have to look closely.

Raw morels contain substances that can cause **poisoning**. Only thorough **cooking** makes them digestible. Dangerous is the confusion with the **false morel**. It also grows in spring, but its cap is **twisted like a brain** instead of honeycomb-like, and it is poisonous. Anyone who gathers mushrooms should therefore always have them checked at a **mushroom inspection**.
Morels form their spores in tiny sacs, the **asci**. That is why they are counted among the **sac fungi**. Most well-known edible mushrooms such as the porcini, by contrast, belong to the club fungi.

Dried morels are especially expensive in the shop. They grow only for a short time in spring and are hard to find. They can also only be cultivated with great effort. Dried, they keep a strong, spicy aroma.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities there are official mushroom inspectors who check gathered mushrooms.
Morels often turn up in places where a fire has burned before.

teile.einleitung: Firs are evergreen conifers with soft, flat needles and upright cones. In Switzerland, the silver fir grows wild in many forests. As a Christmas tree, a fir stands every year in countless living rooms.
wichtigste: Firs are conifers and belong to the pine family.
The silver fir grows wild in Swiss forests.
The cones of the fir stand upright on the twig.
On the underside of fir needles you can see two white stripes.
Fir needles are flat and do not prick.
The fir is often decorated as a Christmas tree.
With its deep taproot, the fir stands very firmly in the ground.

abschnitte.text: The **silver fir** can grow 30 to 50 metres tall and several hundred years old. Its bark is pale grey and smooth for a long time, which is where the name comes from. The needles are flat, slightly notched at the tip and feel soft. On the underside they have two white **wax stripes**, in which the stomata lie.

The cones of the fir stand **upright** like candles on the uppermost twigs. When the seeds are ripe, the scales fall off one by one and the wind carries the winged seeds away. Only a bare spindle is left standing on the twig. That is why you almost never find whole fir cones on the forest floor, and most “fir cones” really come from the **spruce**.

The silver fir grows mainly on the Central Plateau, in the Jura and in the Pre-Alps, often mixed with beeches and spruces. It tolerates a lot of **shade** and, as a young tree, can wait for decades under big trees. In the Emmental it shapes the famous selection forests, in which young and old trees stand side by side. It is among the most common tree species in Switzerland.

Roe deer and red deer very much like to eat the buds of young firs. Many small trees do not survive this **browsing damage**, which is why foresters sometimes surround them with protective sleeves. Against drought, the fir is more robust than the spruce thanks to its deep **taproot**. That is why it is regarded as an important tree for forests in climate change.

abschnitte.titel: The fir as a Christmas tree
abschnitte.text: The custom of putting up a decorated conifer at Christmas spread in the 19th century. Today the **Nordmann fir** from the Caucasus is the most popular Christmas tree, because it keeps its needles for a long time. Many Christmas trees come from special plantations. In Switzerland, many trees are sold from native forests and plantations.

Fir wood is pale, light and easy to work. It is used for roof frames, boards, furniture and wooden shingles. Because it contains hardly any **resin**, it is also suitable for structures in water. Wreaths and Advent arrangements are bound from fir twigs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tree with needle-shaped leaves that mostly stays green in winter too
The woody fruiting body of conifers in which the seeds ripen
A strong main root that grows vertically deep into the ground
Damage when animals eat the buds and shoots of young trees

gewusst: You almost never find whole fir cones on the ground, because they fall apart on the tree.
A saying to remember it: the spruce is spiky, the fir is not.
A young fir can stay small for over 100 years in the shade and then still grow into a giant.

teile.einleitung: Urban trees grow along streets, in squares and in parks. They give shade, cool the air and are a habitat for animals. At the same time, they have a much harder time in the city than in the forest.
wichtigste: Urban trees cool the city because they evaporate water through their leaves.
This process is called transpiration.
Road salt and compacted soil harm the roots.
Common urban trees are plane, lime, maple, horse chestnut and ginkgo.
The silver lime is regarded as a heat-tolerant urban tree of the future.
Many cities keep a tree register, a list of all urban trees.

abschnitte.text: Trees make a city more pleasant. Their crowns give **shade** and hold dust back from the air. Through their leaves they evaporate a lot of water, a process called **transpiration**. This cools the surroundings, much as sweating cools the body. In addition, urban trees offer birds, insects and squirrels a habitat.

In the city, trees often have little room for their roots. The soil is **compacted** by cars and people: it has hardly any pores, so the roots lack air and water. In winter, **road salt** gets into the soil with the meltwater and damages roots and leaves. The trees then take up water and nutrients less well. On top of that come heat, exhaust fumes and injuries from vehicles.

The **plane tree** is recognised by its patchy bark, which flakes off in plates. Limes, maples and horse chestnuts also often stand along streets. With the **ginkgo**, male trees are usually planted, because the seeds of female trees smell very unpleasant. The leaves of the horse chestnut often turn brown as early as summer. The cause is the **horse chestnut leaf miner**, whose caterpillars feed inside the leaves.

Summers are getting hotter and drier. Spruces and silver firs suffer greatly from this. That is why cities are increasingly planting species that tolerate heat better. The **silver lime** comes from south-eastern Europe and is regarded as such a tree of the future. So that urban gardeners keep an overview, many cities keep a **tree register**: a list of all urban trees with species, location and condition.

gewusst: On a hot summer day, a large tree can evaporate several hundred litres of water.
The ginkgo is regarded as a living fossil: its relatives grew as long ago as the time of the dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: A drupe is a fruit with juicy flesh and a hard stone in the middle. Cherries, plums and peaches are well-known examples.
wichtigste: The cherry is a drupe.
The hard stone arises from the inner fruit wall.
The seed is inside the stone.
Mango, olive and coconut are drupes too.
With the almond, we eat the seed.
Cherry, plum and apricot belong to the rose family.

abschnitte.text: The wall of a drupe has three layers. On the outside is a thin **skin**. Beneath it lies the juicy **flesh**, which we eat. The **inner fruit wall** becomes hard and forms the **stone**. Inside the stone is the **seed**, from which a new tree can grow. The stone protects the seed well.

In everyday speech, fruits such as **cherries**, **plums**, **peaches** and **apricots** are together called **stone fruit**. Their trees all belong to the **rose family**. In Switzerland stone fruit is important: many apricots grow in the Valais, and cherries from the Zug and Basel region are well known. **Kirsch** is also distilled from cherries.

Tropical fruits can also be drupes, such as the **mango** with its large, flat stone. The **olive** is also a drupe. Olive oil is pressed from it. Even the **coconut**, despite its name, is not a true nut but a drupe. Its hard shell is the stone, and the white flesh belongs to the seed.

The **almond** is related to the peach. Its fruit looks like a small, green, furry peach. The flesh, however, is leathery and dry and is not eaten. What we buy as an almond is the **seed** from the stone. With cherries and plums, by contrast, we eat the flesh and throw the stone away.

gewusst: The coconut is one of the largest drupes of all.
Cherry stone pillows are warmed up and give off warmth for a long time.

teile.einleitung: The porcini is one of the best known and best loved edible mushrooms. You find it in summer and autumn in the forest, often under spruces and beeches.
wichtigste: The porcini is a very popular edible mushroom.
Under the cap it has tubes like a sponge.
Its stem is thick and bulbous.
The flesh is white and stays white when cut open.
It is often found under spruces and beeches.
Another name for it is the king bolete.

abschnitte.text: The porcini has a brown, domed **cap**. Under the cap it has no gills but **tubes**, which look like a sponge. In young mushrooms they are whitish, later yellowish to olive green. The **stem** is thick and bulbous and often has a fine, pale net pattern. If you cut the mushroom open, the flesh is **white**.

Porcini grow in the forest, often under **spruces** and **beeches**, but also under pines and oaks. The mushroom lives together with the trees: its fine web in the soil is joined to the tree roots. The mushroom helps the tree take up water and nutrients. In return, it gets sugar from the tree. Without its tree, the porcini cannot grow.

The porcini is regarded as an especially fine **edible mushroom**. That is why it is also called the **gentleman’s mushroom**. You can fry it, put it in sauces or risotto, or dry it. Dried porcini have a strong aroma. Good to know: the similar **bitter bolete** is very bitter and can spoil a whole dish.

Anyone who gathers mushrooms must know them very well, because some mushrooms are poisonous. In Switzerland, you can show gathered mushrooms at a **mushroom inspection**. Many municipalities offer this. Experts look at every mushroom and say whether it may be eaten. In some cantons there are also rules on how many mushrooms you may gather and on which days.

gewusst: A porcini can weigh more than a kilogram.
To this day, porcini can hardly be cultivated, because they need living trees.

teile.einleitung: Dew is the little drops of water that glitter on grass, leaves and spider webs on cool mornings. It does not fall from the sky like rain, but forms right where it lies. That is why it is counted as deposited precipitation.
wichtigste: Dew is made of small drops of water that form on the grass on cool mornings.
Dew forms when damp air cools down on cold surfaces.
The water vapour in the air condenses into drops.
The temperature at which this happens is called the dew point.
There is most dew after clear, windless nights.
If it is below freezing, frost forms instead of dew.
Some plants and animals in deserts live on dew.

abschnitte.text: **Dew** is water that settles out of the invisible moisture in the air onto surfaces. You find it mostly early in the morning on meadows, car windows and spider webs. Because it does not fall from clouds, it is called **deposited precipitation**. Frost and hoarfrost also belong to this group.

On clear nights, the ground and plants give off heat into the sky and cool down a lot. The air directly above them cools down as well. Cold air can hold less water vapour than warm air. When it reaches the **dew point**, the water vapour turns into liquid water, which is called **condensation**.

abschnitte.titel: When is there a lot of dew?
abschnitte.text: Most dew forms after nights without clouds and without wind. Clouds act like a blanket and hold the heat in, so the ground stays warmer. Wind mixes the air and stops it from cooling down strongly near the ground. There is especially a lot of dew in late summer and autumn, when the air is damp and the nights are getting longer.

If the temperature of the surface is below freezing, no drops form, but fine ice crystals instead. This white coating is called **frost**. When drops of dew freeze afterwards, it is called frozen dew. In winter you often see frost on meadows, roofs and car windows.

Dew is an important source of water for many living things. In the Namib Desert in Africa, beetles catch drops of fog and dew on their backs and drink them. Snails and earthworms like to be out and about when the grass is wet with dew. The drops on the edges of leaves in the morning are often not dew at all, but water that the plant gives off itself, called **guttation**.

You experience the same principle when a cold bottle from the fridge gets wet on the outside. Glasses also mist up when you come into a warm room from outside in winter. The drops of dew on a field usually supply only very little water, less than a millimetre per night. Even so, meadows can be so wet in the morning that your shoes get soaked through.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which the water vapour in the air turns into drops
The change from water vapour to liquid water
Water as an invisible gas in the air
Ice crystals that form when it is freezing instead of dew

gewusst: Dew likes to form on blades of grass, because thin blades cool down especially quickly at night.
A desert beetle in the Namib stretches up into the fog in the morning so that drops of water run into its mouth.
People used to believe that dew fell from the sky like rain.

teile.einleitung: Simon Schwendener was a Swiss botanist from the St Gallen Rhine Valley. He studied how plants are built inside and made a famous discovery about lichens.
wichtigste: Simon Schwendener was born in 1829 in Buchs in the canton of St Gallen.
He worked in Munich as an assistant to Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli.
Around 1867 he recognised that lichens consist of a fungus and an alga.
Many lichen researchers at first rejected this explanation fiercely.
From 1878 he taught in Berlin and headed the Botanical Institute there for over three decades.
He compared the strengthening tissues of plants with girders in building.

abschnitte.titel: From the Rhine Valley into the world
abschnitte.text: Simon Schwendener was born in 1829 in **Buchs** in the St Gallen Rhine Valley. He worked in Munich as assistant to the Swiss botanist **Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli**. Together they wrote the textbook “The Microscope”. Later Schwendener taught in Basel and Tübingen. From 1878 he was professor in **Berlin**.

Lichens grow on stones, bark and walls. For a long time they were thought to be independent living things. Around 1867 Schwendener showed that a lichen consists of a **fungus** and an **alga** that live together. Many lichen researchers fought this view for a long time. Today such partnerships are called **symbiosis**, and Schwendener’s view is regarded as correct.

In his work on the **mechanical principle** in the structure of plants, Schwendener showed something astonishing. The **strengthening tissues** in stems are arranged as an engineer would arrange girders in a building. In this way thin stalks stay flexible and yet stable. With this he founded the technical mechanics of plants.

Schwendener also studied **leaf arrangement**, that is, how the leaves are arranged on the shoot. He explained the regular patterns by the pressure that young leaf buds exert on one another. He also researched the **guard cells** of the stomata. He explained their movement by the structure of their cell walls.

gewusst: Schwendener headed the Botanical Institute in Berlin for over three decades.
His explanation of lichens was at first attacked and is today part of the basic knowledge of biology.

teile.einleitung: A keystone species is a species of animal or plant that is much more important to its ecosystem than its abundance would suggest. If it disappears, the whole community of living things changes greatly.
wichtigste: The term keystone species was coined by Robert Paine in 1969.
Without the sea star Pisaster, mussels spread and the number of species fell.
The influence of a keystone species is much greater than its abundance.
The beaver reshapes waters as an ecosystem engineer.
Elephants keep the savanna open.
Many other animals use the holes of the black woodpecker.

abschnitte.text: The American zoologist **Robert Paine** coined the term **keystone species** in 1969. He compared an especially influential species with the **keystone** of a stone arch. This stone at the top in the middle holds the whole arch together. A keystone species can be rare and yet shape the structure of a community of living things.

On the rocky coast in the north-west of the USA, Paine repeatedly removed the sea star **Pisaster** from the rocks. This sea star prefers to eat **mussels**. Without it, the mussels overgrew the rocks and crowded out many other species. The **number of species** fell clearly. In this way Paine showed how important a single predator can be.

The **beaver** was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. From the middle of the 20th century it was reintroduced. It is regarded as an **ecosystem engineer**: with dams it dams up streams and creates ponds, wetlands and **dead wood**. Many amphibians, insects and fish benefit from this. The **black woodpecker** is also important in Swiss forests. Its large holes are later used by, for example, stock doves, Tengmalm’s owls, bats or wild bees.

abschnitte.titel: Examples from all over the world
abschnitte.text: **African elephants** eat bushes and push over trees. In this way they prevent **scrub encroachment** and keep the savanna open. **Prairie dogs** in North America dig large burrow systems, loosen the soil and offer shelter to other animals. **Fig trees** in tropical forests bear fruit even in times of scarcity. They are therefore called a **keystone resource** for fruit-eating animals.

gewusst: A single beaver dam can turn a stream into a whole landscape of ponds.
Because fig trees fruit at different times, there are almost always ripe figs somewhere.

teile.einleitung: The taiga is a huge coniferous forest in the far north of the Earth. It stretches through Russia, Scandinavia, Canada and Alaska. The winters there are long and icy cold, the summers short.
wichtigste: The taiga is the largest continuous belt of forest on Earth.
A huge part lies in Siberia in Russia.
Mainly spruces, pines, firs and larches grow there.
The elk, or moose, is the largest deer in the world and lives in the taiga.
The brown bear and the Siberian tiger also live in the taiga.

abschnitte.text: The taiga is also called **boreal coniferous forest**, boreal meaning northern. It forms a broad belt around the north of the Earth. A huge part lies in **Siberia** in Russia, where it stretches over thousands of kilometres. Other large areas lie in Canada, Alaska and Scandinavia. The winters last many months and are very cold.

In the taiga grow mainly **conifers** such as spruce, pine, fir and larch. Their needles lose little water and tolerate frost. The **larch** even sheds its needles in autumn. In between grow birches and poplars. In some areas the ground is frozen deep down all year round, which is called **permafrost**.
