The solar wind is usually between about 400 and 800 kilometres per second fast. It therefore needs only two to four days to reach the Earth. It blows far beyond the planets and forms a huge bubble, the **heliosphere**. The space probe Voyager 1 left this bubble in 2012.

The Earth has a magnetic field that acts like an invisible shield. This region is called the **magnetosphere**. It steers most of the particles of the solar wind around the Earth. Without this protection, the solar wind would slowly strip away our atmosphere, as happened on Mars.

At the poles, some particles can penetrate into the upper atmosphere. There they make oxygen and nitrogen glow, green, red or violet. This is how **auroras** arise, called the northern lights in the north. In very strong solar storms, for example in May 2024, they could even be seen in Switzerland.

Sometimes the Sun ejects huge clouds of particles, so-called **coronal mass ejections**. If they hit the Earth, a geomagnetic storm results. Such storms can disturb satellites, GPS and radio and even damage power grids. In 1989, as a result, the power went out for hours in the Canadian province of Quebec.

The solar wind was predicted in the 1950s by the physicist Eugene Parker. The space probe **Parker Solar Probe** has flown since 2018 closer to the Sun than any probe before. Already at the Moon landing in 1969, the astronauts set up a solar wind sail from the University of Bern. With this aluminium foil, particles of the solar wind were caught and later studied.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost, very hot layer of the Sun’s atmosphere.
The region around the Earth that its magnetic field protects.
Coloured glowing in the sky caused by particles from the Sun.
The huge bubble in space that the solar wind forms around the solar system.

gewusst: The Bernese solar wind sail was the only non-American experiment on the first Moon landing.
The tails of comets always point away from the Sun, because the solar wind blows them away.
Through the solar wind, the Sun loses about a million tonnes of material every second.

teile.einleitung: A cutting is a piece cut off a plant that forms new roots. In this way you can propagate plants entirely without seeds. The new plant is exactly like the mother plant.
wichtigste: A cutting is a plant part from which a new plant grows.
The new roots are called adventitious roots.
Tip cuttings are cut just below a node.
Rooting hormone products mostly contain plant hormones from the group of auxins.
A cover with moist air protects the cutting from drying out.
Willows root especially easily.

abschnitte.text: For a **tip cutting**, you cut off the tip of a shoot, just below a **node**. A node is the place where a leaf sits on the stem. New roots form there especially easily. These roots do not grow from an old root but from the stem. They are called **adventitious roots**.

A fresh cutting has no roots yet, so it can hardly take up water. Through its leaves, however, it keeps evaporating water. If it keeps too many leaves, it easily **dries out**. That is why the lower leaves are removed. Cuttings are often placed under a **cover** or film. The moist air beneath stops them from losing too much water.

Gardeners sometimes dip cuttings in a **rooting hormone product**. It mostly contains plant hormones from the group of **auxins**. These substances encourage the plant to form roots faster. Warmth, light and loose, moist soil are also important. After a few weeks, new leaves show that the cutting has taken.

Not only shoot tips are suitable. The **African violet** is classically propagated with **leaf cuttings**: a single leaf with its stalk goes into the soil. With **willows**, a leafless piece of twig is enough, a **hardwood cutting**, which is stuck in the ground in winter. From a piece of root comes a **root cutting**. All the plants obtained in this way are exact copies of the mother plant.

gewusst: Many fruit varieties and grapevines have been propagated without seeds for a very long time, so that they stay the same.
A willow twig can even form roots in a vase of water.

teile.einleitung: The stratosphere is the second layer of the Earth’s atmosphere, lying at roughly 10 to 50 kilometres in height. In it is the ozone layer, which protects us from dangerous UV radiation. Weather balloons fly here, and sometimes even aeroplanes.
wichtigste: The stratosphere is the second layer of the atmosphere, above the troposphere.
It extends from about 8 to 18 kilometres in height up to roughly 50 kilometres.
The ozone layer is in the stratosphere.
The ozone layer filters dangerous UV radiation from the Sun.
Unlike in the layer below, it gets warmer upwards in the stratosphere.
There are almost no clouds and no weather there.

abschnitte.text: The **atmosphere** consists of several layers like an onion. At the very bottom lies the **troposphere**, in which we live and where the weather takes place. Above it, from about 8 kilometres at the poles and 18 kilometres at the equator, comes the stratosphere. It ends at a height of roughly 50 kilometres, and above that the mesosphere begins.

In the stratosphere lies the **ozone layer**, especially dense at about 15 to 35 kilometres in height. Ozone is a gas made of three oxygen atoms. It swallows a large part of the dangerous **UV radiation** of the Sun. Without this protection, sunburn and skin cancer would be much more common, and life on land would hardly be possible.

In the troposphere it gets colder and colder going up, down to about minus 55 degrees. In the stratosphere it is the other way round, and the temperature rises again going up. The reason is the ozone, which absorbs UV radiation and warms up as it does so. At the upper limit it is about as warm as freezing point.

In the 1980s, researchers discovered an **ozone hole** over Antarctica. The cause was gases such as **CFCs**, which were in spray cans and refrigerators. In 1987, many countries decided in the Montreal Protocol to ban these substances. Since then, the ozone layer has been slowly recovering, and it is expected to be largely healed again around the middle of the 21st century.

Large passenger aeroplanes mostly fly at 10 to 12 kilometres, often at the boundary with the stratosphere. There are hardly any clouds there and little turbulence. Weather balloons rise to over 30 kilometres and measure temperature and wind. The Swiss scientist Auguste **Piccard** rose in 1931 as the first human in a balloon into the stratosphere, to almost 16 kilometres.

In Arosa in Graubünden, the thickness of the ozone layer has been measured since 1926. This is the longest series of measurements in the world for it. Today **MeteoSwiss** continues these measurements, among other places in Davos. Thanks to such data, we know exactly how the ozone layer has changed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The envelope of air that surrounds the Earth.
A gas made of three oxygen atoms that swallows UV radiation.
Invisible sunlight that can cause sunburn.
Gases that used to be in spray cans and destroy the ozone layer.

gewusst: If you pressed all the ozone of the stratosphere together at ground-level pressure, the layer would be only about three millimetres thick.
The name stratosphere comes from the Latin word stratum, meaning layer.
Auguste Piccard was the model for Professor Calculus in the Tintin comics.

teile.einleitung: The pedunculate oak is one of the most important trees in Europe and is also widespread in Switzerland. It can grow very old and mighty and is a home for countless animals.
wichtigste: The pedunculate oak is so called because its acorns hang on long stalks.
Each acorn sits in a small cup.
The ripe acorns fall from the tree in autumn.
Wild boar like to eat acorns very much.
The jay hides acorns and so helps to plant new oaks.
A great many insect species live on an old oak.

abschnitte.text: The pedunculate oak can grow over 30 metres tall and several hundred years old. The bark of an old oak is **thick and deeply furrowed**. The leaves have rounded lobes at the edge. The pedunculate oak gets its name from its fruits: the **acorns hang on long stalks**. In the similar sessile oak, by contrast, the acorns sit almost directly on the twig.

An acorn sits in a small **cup**, like an egg in an egg cup. **In autumn** the ripe acorns fall from the tree. For many forest animals they are important food. **Wild boar** especially like to eat them, but so do squirrels and mice. The **jay**, a colourful crow-family bird, hides acorns in the ground as a winter store. The forgotten acorns germinate, and so new oaks grow.

An old oak is a huge habitat. **A great many insect species** live on it, as many as on hardly any other tree. Beetles such as the stag beetle, caterpillars of butterflies and wasps find food here. Birds and bats live in tree holes. On the leaves you sometimes find round balls, the **oak galls**. They arise when small gall wasps lay their eggs in the leaf.

Oak wood is hard, heavy and long-lasting. In the past, houses, ships and bridges were built from it. Furniture and parquet floors are also often made of oak. **Oak wood** is also used to make **wine barrels**. The wood gives the wine a special flavour. In Switzerland, foresters are encouraging the oak again today, because it tolerates drought quite well.

gewusst: In the past, ink was made from oak galls.
An oak forms acorns for the first time only after many years.

teile.einleitung: Some plants spread their seeds entirely without help from wind, water or animals. They fling them away themselves or simply let them fall. This is called self-dispersal.
wichtigste: The technical term for self-dispersal is autochory.
Touch-me-not is so called because its fruits burst open when touched.
The tension in the capsules comes from water pressure in the cells.
The squirting cucumber squirts its seeds out of the fruit with sap.
In broom, the drying halves of the pod twist and fling the seeds away.
When heavy fruits simply fall to the ground, this is called barochory.
The seeds mostly land near the parent plant.

abschnitte.text: Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can travel. Many plants use the wind, water or animals for this. In **self-dispersal**, the plant itself makes sure that the seeds get away. The technical term is **autochory**. The word comes from Greek: “auto” means self, “chorein” means to move on.

Touch-me-not gets its name from the fact that you must not touch it. Its ripe capsules are under tension. If you touch them, they burst open in a flash, curl up and fling the seeds away. The tension comes from **water pressure in the cells** of the capsule wall. Experts speak of **turgor**. The introduced Himalayan balsam spreads especially successfully in this way.

The **squirting cucumber** from the Mediterranean region builds up high pressure in its fruits. When the ripe fruit falls off, it squirts the seeds out together with sap. In **broom**, the pods dry in the sun. The two halves of the pod **twist** as they do so, until they burst open with a crack and fling the seeds away.

The **cranesbill** is named after the long, beak-shaped form of its fruit. As it dries, the parts of the fruit tense and snap upwards, flinging the seeds away. **Barochory** manages entirely without a swing: heavy fruits such as horse chestnuts or acorns simply fall to the ground.

Self-dispersal needs no helpers and works reliably. Its **disadvantage**: the seeds mostly land **near the parent plant**, only a few metres away. With the wind, seeds can travel much further. Often, however, a second dispersal is added, for example when ants carry the seeds away or animals hide acorns.

gewusst: The capsules of touch-me-not open in fractions of a second and are among the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.
If you walk past a broom bush in summer, on warm days you can sometimes hear the cracking of the bursting pods.

teile.einleitung: A steppe is a wide, treeless grassland. Steppes occur where it is too dry for forests but too moist for deserts. The largest steppe in the world stretches right across Europe and Asia.
wichtigste: Hardly any trees grow in steppes, because too little rain falls.
The Eurasian Steppe reaches from Eastern Europe to East Asia.
Under steppes, the very fertile chernozem arose.
Today wheat is grown on many former steppe soils.
Mongolia is strongly shaped by steppes.
The Przewalski’s horse was reintroduced to the Mongolian steppe.

abschnitte.text: In the steppe grow mainly **grasses** and herbs. There are hardly any trees, because **too little rain** falls. The summers are often hot and dry, the winters cold. A typical steppe grass is **feather grass**. It has long, feathery awns that wave in the wind. In this way the steppe sometimes looks like a silvery sea.

The largest steppe is the **Eurasian Steppe**. It stretches from Eastern Europe through Kazakhstan to **Mongolia** and China. Similar grasslands exist on other continents: in North America they are called **prairie**, in South America **pampas**. In Switzerland there is no true steppe, but in the dry Valais some steppe plants grow on slopes.

Under the steppes, a very fertile, dark soil has formed over a long time: **chernozem**, or black earth. Part of the grasses die back every year, and their remains turn into humus. That is why the soil is rich in nutrients. Many former steppes are now used as fields, above all for **wheat**. Ukraine is known for this.

In Mongolia, many people still live as **nomads** to this day. They move with their herds across the steppe and live in round tents, the **yurts**. In the steppe there are also wild animals such as marmots, antelopes and birds of prey. The **Przewalski’s horse** had vanished from the wild. With animals from zoos, it was reintroduced to the Mongolian steppe.

gewusst: Przewalski’s horse is regarded as the last true wild horse.
A yurt can be taken down and put up again in a few hours.

teile.einleitung: Sebastian Kneipp was a German priest in the 19th century. He became known because he used cold water for health. His ideas live on to this day in Kneipp facilities, also in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Sebastian Kneipp was a priest and lived in the 19th century.
His cure is associated especially with cold water.
His teaching on health rests on five pillars.
He worked in Bad Wörishofen in the Allgäu.
He described his teaching in the book “My Water Cure”.
Typical of Kneipp facilities is water treading in the stork walk.

abschnitte.text: Sebastian Kneipp was born in **1821** in Swabia in Bavaria and died in **1897**. He came from a poor family of weavers and was determined to become a priest. Later he worked as a **priest** in **Bad Wörishofen** in the Allgäu. There he looked after not only the church but also the sick who came to him.

As a young man, Kneipp fell seriously ill with a lung complaint. By his own account, he read in a book about the healing power of water. He then took **short baths in the cold Danube** in winter. He was convinced that this had cured him. From then on he occupied himself all his life with water treatments.

Kneipp’s teaching rests on **five pillars**. The best known is **water**, for example as affusions, baths or compresses. Added to this are **exercise**, simple, natural **nutrition** and **medicinal plants**, for example as tea. The fifth pillar is a balanced **way of life**, that is, a healthy rhythm of work, rest and sleep.

abschnitte.titel: Water treading in the stork walk
abschnitte.text: In many spa towns, parks and on hiking trails there are **Kneipp facilities**, also in Switzerland. Typical is a basin with cold water. You wade in it in the **stork walk**: with every step you lift one leg completely out of the water. Many people find this refreshing and invigorating. There is often also an **arm bath**, in which you dip your arms into the cold water.

Kneipp wrote down his experiences in the book **“My Water Cure”**. It became a great success and was translated into many languages. Through him Bad Wörishofen became a well-known **spa town**. How strongly individual treatments work is still judged differently today. In the case of illness, the advice of a doctor always belongs with it.

gewusst: In Germany, Kneipp practice is on the list of intangible cultural heritage.
Products such as bath additives and teas are named after Kneipp today.

teile.einleitung: In many lakes the water lies in layers of different temperatures, one on top of another. This is called thermal stratification. It changes with the seasons and is important for the oxygen in the lake and for everything that lives in it.
wichtigste: In summer, warm water lies stably on top of cold water.
The upper layer is called the epilimnion, the deep layer the hypolimnion.
Water is densest at about 4 °C.
Under the ice the colder water lies on top, which is called inverse stratification.
In homothermy the whole lake has the same temperature and can mix.
Because of global warming, summer stratification begins earlier and lasts longer.

abschnitte.text: In summer the sun warms the top layer of water, the **epilimnion**. The **wind** at the surface mixes this layer through, so it usually has an almost uniform temperature. Below it comes the **thermocline**, in which the temperature drops quickly. At the very bottom lies the cold, dense **hypolimnion**. It stays cold all summer and is cut off from exchange with the air.

The phase in which a lake is stably layered in summer is called **summer stagnation**. Warm, light water lies on top of cold, heavy water. The stratification is very stable, even though the difference is only a few degrees. At higher temperatures, the **density** changes more with each degree. That is why the wind needs a great deal of energy to mix the layers.

Water is at its densest at about **4 °C**. That is why water at this temperature sinks downwards. At the bottom of a deep lake that has frozen over, the water in winter is about 4 °C. The colder water close to 0 °C stays directly under the ice. This reversed order is called **inverse stratification**, and it lets fish survive the winter.

In autumn the surface cools down until the whole lake has the same temperature. This state is called **homothermy**. Then there is no difference in density any more, and the wind can turn over the whole lake. As it does so, **oxygen** reaches the depths and nutrients come up to the top. In many lakes this happens in spring and autumn.

**Global warming** also affects Swiss lakes. Warmer surfaces lead to an earlier and more stable summer stratification that lasts longer. This makes mixing in winter harder. As a result, less oxygen reaches the deep water. That can become a problem for fish and other animals in the depths.

gewusst: Because water is heaviest at 4 °C, deep lakes do not freeze through to the bottom.
In very deep lakes it can happen that the water at the bottom does not mix fully with the surface water for years.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is the star around which the Earth orbits, and the centre of our solar system. It is a huge ball of glowing hot gas that gives light and warmth. Without the Sun there would be no life on Earth.
wichtigste: The Sun is the star that lies closest to us.
The Earth orbits the Sun once in a year.
The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from the Earth.
It consists mainly of hydrogen and helium.
In its interior, hydrogen fuses into helium and releases energy.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
You must never look directly at the Sun without protection.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a **star**, an average yellow dwarf among billions of stars in the Milky Way. It only seems so big and bright because it is much closer to us than all the other stars. Its diameter is about 1.4 million kilometres, which is about 109 times the diameter of the Earth. Over a million Earths would fit inside the Sun.

In the core of the Sun there are about 15 million degrees Celsius and enormous pressure. There hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, which is called **nuclear fusion**. In the process an enormous amount of energy is released, which radiates into space as light and heat. The surface, the **photosphere**, at about 5,500 degrees, is much cooler than the core.

Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. The Earth goes round the Sun in about 365 days, which is one year. Plants use the light for **photosynthesis** and so make food and oxygen. The Sun also drives wind, weather and the water cycle.

On the Sun there are dark **sunspots**, which are somewhat cooler than their surroundings. Their number rises and falls in a cycle of about eleven years. In solar storms, the Sun hurls particles into space, which can cause polar lights on Earth. In Locarno-Monti in Ticino, sunspots have been observed regularly since 1957.

Solar panels on roofs turn sunlight into electricity, and in Switzerland there are more every year. The **UV radiation** of the Sun can cause sunburn, so people protect themselves with sun cream, a hat and sunglasses. You should never look directly at the Sun, not even with binoculars. This can damage the eyes for ever.

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge cloud of gas and dust. It has about half of its life behind it. In about five billion years it will swell into a **red giant**. After that a small, slowly cooling white dwarf is left.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge ball of hot gas that shines by itself.
The fusing of small atomic nuclei into larger ones, in which energy is released.
A darker, somewhat cooler area on the surface of the Sun.
The Sun with all the planets, moons and other bodies that orbit it.

gewusst: The Sun contains over 99 per cent of the total mass of our solar system.
The light we see today left the surface of the Sun about eight minutes ago.
The Sun is so big that over a million Earths would fit inside it.

teile.einleitung: A spore print is a picture that a mushroom draws itself on paper. For this you lay the mushroom cap on a sheet and wait. The colour of the spore powder helps in identifying mushrooms.
wichtigste: For a spore print, you cut off the stem and lay the cap, underside down, on paper.
A glass or bowl over it stops a draught from blowing the spores away.
After a few hours or overnight, the print becomes visible.
Paper that is half white and half black shows pale and dark spores.
The colour of the spore powder is an important identifying feature.
The poisonous death cap has white spore powder.

abschnitte.text: First you cut off the **stem**. That way the cap lies flat with its underside on the **paper**. Then you cover it with a **glass** or a bowl. Even a slight **draught** would otherwise smudge the fine pattern. The mushroom drops its spores little by little. That is why you leave it **a few hours** or overnight.

Often a paper is used that is **half white and half black**. White spore powder is hardly visible on white paper. On the dark part it becomes visible. Dark powder, by contrast, can be seen well on the pale part. In this way every colour can be seen clearly.

In a **gill fungus**, the spores fall exactly between the gills. That is why a **radiating** pattern forms that looks like the gills themselves. When the print is finished, you can make it last. A fine mist of **hairspray** or fixative spray sticks the loose powder down.

The **colour of the spore powder** is an important feature in identifying mushrooms. Mushrooms that look similar can often be told apart in this way. The very poisonous **death cap** leaves a **white** print. Button mushrooms, with which it is confused, by contrast have dark spore powder. Even so, the rule is: always have mushrooms for eating checked at a **mushroom inspection**.

gewusst: A spore print can look so beautiful that some people use it to create pictures.
After the experiment you wash your hands well, especially if you have touched an unknown mushroom.

teile.einleitung: Terpenes are a huge group of natural substances. They give many plants their scent, for example citrus fruits, conifers or peppermint. Chemically, they are built from units that each have five carbon atoms.
wichtigste: Terpenes are formally built from isoprene units with 5 carbon atoms.
A monoterpene has 10 carbon atoms.
Sesquiterpenes have 15, tetraterpenes 40 carbon atoms.
Beta-carotene is a tetraterpene.
Limonene smells of citrus fruits.
Natural rubber is a polyterpene.
The word terpene comes from turpentine.

abschnitte.text: Terpenes can be described as a chain of several **isoprene units**. An isoprene has the formula C5H8, so **5 carbon atoms**. This is called the **isoprene rule**. Depending on the number of units, different classes are distinguished. Many tens of thousands of different terpenes are known.

A **monoterpene** consists of two isoprene units and has 10 C atoms. **Sesquiterpenes** have 15 C atoms, and “sesqui” means one and a half. Diterpenes have 20 and triterpenes 30 C atoms. **Tetraterpenes** have 40 C atoms, and they include the carotenoids such as **beta-carotene**. **Polyterpenes** consist of very many units, an example being **natural rubber** from the milky sap of the rubber tree.

Many terpenes smell strong. **Limonene** is the main component of the oils in orange and lemon peel. **Menthol** gives peppermint its freshness. **Pinene** gives pine forests their typical scent. Plants use substances like these to ward off animals that eat them or to attract insects.

When **pine resin** is distilled, **turpentine oil** is produced. It consists mainly of monoterpenes such as pinene and is used as a solvent. What is left behind is **rosin**, which is used, for example, to rub on violin bows. The word “terpene” comes from turpentine. Limonene is also used as a fragrance in cleaning products.

The active building block is called **isopentenyl pyrophosphate**. In the cytoplasm it is made from acetyl-CoA by the **mevalonate pathway**. In the plastids there is also the **MEP pathway**. From these C5 building blocks, enzymes put together the many different terpenes. Animals and humans also use the mevalonate pathway, for example for cholesterol.

gewusst: The bluish haze over large forests is partly caused by terpenes that the trees give off into the air.
Rosin from pine resin makes the violin bow grip the strings and set them sounding.

teile.einleitung: A protection forest protects people, houses, roads and railway lines from natural hazards. It holds back avalanches, rockfall and landslides. In Switzerland, about half of the forest has such a task.
wichtigste: About half of the Swiss forest area counts as protection forest.
Trees hold the snow cover in place and prevent avalanches.
Trunks slow down and stop falling stones.
Roots hold the soil together on steep slopes.
Andermatt protected its ban forest as early as 1397 with a ban charter.
A protection forest needs care so that young trees grow up.

abschnitte.text: According to surveys by the Confederation, **about half** of the Swiss forest area counts as **protection forest**. The share is especially large in the **Alpine cantons**. There, villages, roads and railway lines often lie directly beneath steep slopes. Without the forest, many valleys would be far more dangerous. Protection is therefore one of the most important tasks of the forest in Switzerland.

Trunks and crowns break up the **snow cover**. In this way they prevent it from sliding off as a large slab and causing an **avalanche**. In addition, less snow falls directly on the ground. In **rockfall**, a falling stone hits trunks and loses energy. A dense, healthy forest holds back many stones in this way. Above the forest, **supporting structures** of steel or wood are built to hold the snow cover in place.

On steep slopes, the dense **network of roots** anchors the soil like a net. In this way it prevents **landslides** and **erosion**. The forest soil also stores a lot of **rainwater** and releases it slowly. This also helps against flooding in the streams.

Even in the Middle Ages, people knew how important the forest is. In **1397** the valley people of **Andermatt** issued a **ban charter**. In it, use of the forest above the village was forbidden so that it would protect against avalanches. The **ban forest** of Andermatt is well known to this day.

If only trees of the same age grow in a forest, many can collapse at the same time. **Foresters** therefore create gaps in which **young trees** can grow up. Too many **red deer, roe deer and chamois** can endanger the young growth, because they eat buds and shoots. A well-kept protection forest is much **cheaper** than technical protective structures, which are expensive to build and maintain.

gewusst: A protection forest does its work again every year without having to be rebuilt.
The Confederation and the cantons support the care of protection forests with money.

teile.einleitung: If you look at the cross-section of a tree trunk, you often see a pale outer ring and a darker core. The outer part is called sapwood. It is the still active part of the wood, which carries water from the roots to the crown.
wichtigste: Sapwood is the outer part of the woody body that still conducts water.
Parenchyma cells that store substances still live in the sapwood.
Sapwood contains starch and sugar but hardly any protective substances.
That is why it is more susceptible to fungi and insects than heartwood.
In heartwood species such as larch or pine, the sapwood is paler than the heartwood.
In sapwood trees such as birch or maple, the trunk is uniformly pale.

abschnitte.titel: The living part of the wood
abschnitte.text: The **sapwood** lies on the outside of the woody body, directly under the bark and phloem. It conducts **water** from the roots up to the crown. Almost all wood cells are dead after a short time. Only the **parenchyma cells** in the sapwood still live for a few years and store substances. In time the sapwood passes inwards into **heartwood** or ripewood.

In **heartwood species** such as oak, larch, pine or black locust, dark substances are deposited in the interior. The sapwood stays **paler** and is clearly set off. In **sapwood trees** such as birch, maple, alder or hornbeam, there is no clearly set-off heartwood. The cross-section is uniformly pale. In spruce and fir, the sapwood is very moist and the inner part of the trunk clearly drier.

Sapwood stores reserve substances such as **starch** and **sugar**. These attract fungi and insects. Protective substances such as **tannins**, which occur in heartwood, are largely missing from it. In pine, the **blue-stain fungus** often grows in the sapwood. It stains the wood blue-grey but hardly reduces its strength.

How long wood lasts outdoors is called **durability**. It is stated for the heartwood. Sapwood is regarded in almost all species as **not very durable**. That is why it is often removed or especially protected in outdoor building parts, for example fences or terraces.

gewusst: In birch and maple you see no dark heartwood on the cross-section, and the whole trunk is pale.
Blue-stained pine wood is usually still almost as strong as unstained wood.

teile.einleitung: A symbiosis is a close partnership between two different kinds of living things. Often both partners benefit from it, like fungi and tree roots or bacteria in the roots of beans. Without such partnerships, many forests, meadows and even we humans would not exist as we know them.
wichtigste: A symbiosis is the close living together of different species.
A relationship from which both partners benefit is called mutualism.
The symbiosis between fungi and plant roots is called mycorrhiza.
Rhizobia form root nodules with legumes and fix nitrogen.
A lichen consists of a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium.
Mistletoe is a hemiparasite that takes water from its host tree.
Useful bacteria also live in the human gut in symbiosis with us.

abschnitte.text: The word **symbiosis** comes from Greek and means living together. In biology it refers to the close living together of two different species. If both partners benefit from it, it is called **mutualism**. In everyday speech, symbiosis usually means exactly this kind of partnership for mutual advantage.

Most land plants work together with fungi, which is called **mycorrhiza**. The fine fungal threads, the **hyphae**, fetch water and minerals such as phosphorus from the soil and pass them on to the plant. In return, the fungus receives sugar from the plant’s photosynthesis. In ectomycorrhiza, which is common in spruce and beech, the fungus forms a mantle of hyphae around the root tips, and porcini and fly agarics belong to it.

Bacteria called **rhizobia** live in small nodules on the roots of legumes such as beans, peas, clover and lentils. They fix nitrogen from the air and make it usable for the plant. Because oxygen disturbs nitrogen fixation, the nodule contains leghaemoglobin. It keeps the oxygen level low, so protecting nitrogen fixation, and colours the inside of the nodules reddish.

A **lichen** is a community of living things made of a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus forms the protective framework and holds water. The alga carries out photosynthesis and supplies sugar. Together, lichens can survive on bare rock, tree bark and even in the high Alps.

Not every way of living together benefits both sides. In **parasitism**, only one partner profits, and the other is harmed. Mistletoe is a **hemiparasite**, because it takes water and minerals from its host tree but carries out photosynthesis itself. When one partner has only advantages and does not bother the other, it is called commensalism.

The clownfish lives among the stinging arms of the **sea anemone** and is protected there from enemies. In return, it chases away fish that want to eat the anemone. Bees and flowers also form a partnership, because the bees get nectar and in return pollinate the flowers. In the gut of cows, micro-organisms help to digest the hard grass.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living together in which both partners have an advantage.
Partnership between fungi and plant roots.
Community of living things made of a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium.
A living thing that lives at the expense of another.
The living thing that serves another as partner or victim.

gewusst: Through a network of fungal threads in the forest soil, trees can exchange nutrients indirectly.
In your gut live roughly as many bacterial cells as your body has cells of its own.
Lichens often grow only a few millimetres a year and can become very old.

teile.einleitung: Summer grazing means that cows, young cattle, sheep and goats spend the summer on an alp. In Switzerland an alpine summer lasts about three months. Summer grazing is important for farms, for the landscape and for biodiversity.
wichtigste: The animals usually go up to the alp in June and return in September.
An alpine summer lasts about 100 days.
A normal stocking unit corresponds to one cow grazing 100 days on the alp.
How many animals an alp may have depends on the supply of feed.
While the animals are up there, winter fodder is harvested in the valley.
Grazed alps become less overgrown with scrub and stay rich in species.
Livestock guardian dogs protect sheep from the wolf.

abschnitte.text: When the snow has melted in early summer and the grass is growing, the **ascent to the alp** begins. This is usually in **June**. The animals then spend about 100 days in the mountains. In September they move back down into the valley, often with decorated cows in the **descent from the alp**. On the alp, alpine herders, dairymen and shepherds look after the animals.

abschnitte.titel: Good for the farm in the valley
abschnitte.text: While the animals are on the alp, the meadows grow in the valley. The farming families harvest **hay** and silage there. The animals need this fodder in winter in the barn. Without summer grazing, many farms would have too little winter fodder. On many alps, **alpine cheese** is also made from the milk.

How many animals an alp can feed is measured in **normal stocking units**, or “Normalstösse”. One normal stocking unit corresponds to one livestock unit, roughly one cow grazing 100 days on the alp. Each alp has a fixed **stocking level** that suits the growth of grass. In this way the pasture is not overused. The **summer grazing payments** made by the Confederation are also based on these figures.

Without grazing, on many alps first shrubs and later forest grow. People say the alp becomes **overgrown with scrub**. Open alpine pastures offer a habitat for many flowers, butterflies and other insects. Summer grazing therefore helps to preserve **biodiversity**. It also shapes the typical picture of the Swiss mountain landscape.

Besides cows and young cattle, many **sheep** spend the summer in the mountains. They can also graze in very steep terrain. Since the wolf has returned, shepherds protect their flocks with fences and **livestock guardian dogs**. These dogs live with the sheep and drive off wolves. Hikers should not disturb them and should walk calmly past the flock.

gewusst: The word “Stoss”, a unit of alpine pasture, is very old: in the past it was used to divide grazing rights among the members of the alp co-operative.
On some alps, goats, horses or pigs also spend the summer.

teile.einleitung: In the history of the Earth there have been five great mass extinctions, in which a large share of all species disappeared in a short time. Many researchers are of the opinion that a sixth has begun today, caused mainly by humans.
wichtigste: Before the present one there were five great mass extinctions, the “Big Five”.
A mass extinction is spoken of when about three quarters of species disappear in a geologically short time.
The greatest mass extinction occurred at the end of the Permian.
66 million years ago, an asteroid impact ended the age of the dinosaurs.
Today’s loss of species is caused mainly by humans.
The dodo and the passenger pigeon are well-known examples of extinct birds.

abschnitte.text: Species die out again and again, and this belongs to the development of life. In a **mass extinction**, however, very many species disappear at the same time in a geologically short period. According to the usual definition, it is **about three quarters** of all species. “Short” in the history of the Earth, however, often means thousands or even millions of years.

Experts distinguish **five great mass extinctions**. The first happened about **445 million years ago** at the end of the **Ordovician**. It was linked with an ice age and a falling sea level. Mass extinctions followed in the Devonian and at the end of the **Permian**. This was the greatest: at that time most of all marine species disappeared. After that came the extinction at the end of the Triassic and at the end of the Cretaceous.

The best-known mass extinction happened **66 million years ago**. A large **asteroid** struck the Earth, in the area of today’s Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. Dust and soot darkened the sky, and the climate changed greatly. The dinosaurs died out, except for one group: from it came today’s **birds**. After that the mammals spread.

The **dodo** was a large, flightless bird on the island of **Mauritius**. After the arrival of humans and the animals they brought with them, it died out in the **17th century**. It became a symbol of the loss of species. The **passenger pigeon** was once the commonest species of bird in North America. Through hunting on a massive scale and forest clearance it disappeared. The last passenger pigeon died in **1914** in a zoo.

Today species die out much faster than the natural average. The main causes are the destruction of habitats, overuse, introduced species, pollution and **climate change**. Unlike in the past, then, it is above all **humans** who are the cause. Whether one can already speak of a true mass extinction is debated. In Switzerland, too, the **Red Lists** show that many species are threatened.

gewusst: The journalist Elizabeth Kolbert won the Pulitzer Prize in 2015 for her book “The Sixth Extinction” about today’s loss of species.
The extinction at the end of the Permian is often called “the Great Dying”.

teile.einleitung: A summergreen deciduous forest bears green leaves in summer and stands bare in winter. Such forests grow where there is a temperate climate with four seasons. Without people, the Swiss Central Plateau, too, would be largely covered by them.
wichtigste: In the summergreen deciduous forest, the trees shed their leaves in autumn.
The climate is temperate, with warm summers, cool winters and rain all year round.
On the Swiss Central Plateau, without people, mainly beech forests would grow.
Beech forests in Ticino have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage since 2021.
Early-flowering plants such as the wood anemone use the light before the leaves come out.
Nutrient-rich humus forms from the leaf litter.

abschnitte.text: The **summergreen deciduous forest** grows in areas with a **temperate climate**. The summers are warm, the winters cool, and rain falls spread over the whole year. In autumn the trees shed their leaves and rest in winter. Such forests exist in Europe, in the **east of the USA** and in East Asia. There they glow in magnificent colours in autumn.

Without clearing, the **Central Plateau** would be largely covered by mixed deciduous forests, above all **beech forests**. Today fields, meadows and settlements shape the landscape. When deciduous and coniferous trees grow together, it is called a **mixed forest**. Mixed forests are usually more resistant to storms and pests. Since 2021, beech forests in **Ticino**, for example in the Valle di Lodano, have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the ancient beech forests of Europe.

abschnitte.titel: Early flowers on the forest floor
abschnitte.text: In spring the trees are still bare. Then a lot of light falls on the forest floor. **Early-flowering plants** such as the **wood anemone** use this short time for flowering and growth. As soon as the leaf canopy is closed, it becomes shady on the ground. Many early flowers then withdraw into their bulbs or rhizomes.

The fallen leaves do not just lie there. Worms, fungi and bacteria break them down. From this, dark, nutrient-rich **humus** forms. Many fungi also live closely with tree roots. This partnership is called **mycorrhiza**: the fungus supplies water and minerals, and the tree gives sugar in return.

Many animals live in the deciduous forest, for example roe deer, foxes, squirrels and numerous birds. The **great spotted woodpecker** drums on tree trunks with its beak. It hammers holes into the wood and searches in them for insects. With loud drumming it also marks its territory in spring.

gewusst: The beech is the most common broadleaved tree in the Swiss forest.
Under a deciduous forest, the ground can be covered in spring with wood anemones like a white carpet.

teile.einleitung: Snow is frozen precipitation made up of tiny ice crystals. It forms high up in the clouds and falls to the ground as flakes. In Switzerland, snow shapes the winter, tourism and even our water supply.
wichtigste: Snow is made up of tiny ice crystals.
It forms in clouds when water vapour freezes in the cold.
Fresh snow consists to a large extent of air.
Snow insulates well and protects plants and animals from frost.
In the Alps, snow can set off avalanches.
Melting snow fills rivers and lakes in spring.

abschnitte.text: In clouds there are tiny water droplets and water vapour. When it is colder than zero degrees, the vapour attaches itself to dust particles and forms **ice crystals**. The crystals grow, hook together and become **snowflakes**. When they are heavy enough, they fall, and if it stays cold enough below, they arrive as snow.

In the Alps much more snow falls than on the Central Plateau. On high mountains it stays all year, above the **snow line**, which in the Swiss Alps is usually at around 2,500 to 3,000 metres. **Glaciers** form from old snow that is pressed together over the years. In Davos, the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF studies snow.

Fresh **powder snow** is light and loose and ideal for skiing. Wet snow is heavy and sticky, and good snowmen are built from it. If snow is melted and refrozen several times, grainy **firn** forms. Snowflakes are white because the light is thrown back in all directions by the many crystal faces.

On steep slopes, a layer of snow can slide off and thunder down into the valley as an **avalanche**. In winter the SLF issues an avalanche bulletin every day. It gives the danger level from 1 (low) to 5 (very high). Anyone who goes off the pistes needs training and emergency equipment.

Snow is very important for winter sports and tourism in Switzerland. Where too little falls, snow cannons produce **artificial snow**. In spring the snow melts and feeds streams, rivers and reservoirs for hydroelectric power. Because of climate change, snow lies less often at low altitudes today than it used to.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, regularly shaped piece of frozen water.
Snow that has just fallen.
A large mass of snow that crashes down a slope.
Old, grainy snow that has thawed and frozen several times.

gewusst: Fresh new snow can consist of over 90 per cent air.
Snow squeaks under your shoes in great cold because the crystals break.
A thick blanket of snow keeps the ground beneath it much warmer than the air above.

teile.einleitung: The basidiomycetes, scientifically Basidiomycota, are a large group of fungi. They include many well-known edible mushrooms such as the porcini, but also rust fungi, which harm plants.
wichtigste: Basidiomycetes form their spores on the outside of club-shaped basidia.
A typical basidium bears four spores.
The spore-forming layer is called the hymenium.
Clamp connections on the hyphae are a typical feature.
The long-lived mycelium is mostly dikaryotic, that is, it has paired nuclei.
Basidiomycetes include the porcini as well as rust and smut fungi.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the **basidia**, the “standing cells”. These are club-shaped cells on whose **outside** the spores arise. A typical basidium bears **four** spores on small stalks. In mushrooms with caps, the basidia lie close together in a layer, the **hymenium**. It covers the **gills** or lines the **tubes** under the cap.

The actual fungus lives invisibly in the soil or in wood. It consists of fine threads, the **hyphae**, which together form the **mycelium**. The fruiting body that we see is only a small part of it. Many basidiomycetes have small bridges on their hyphae, the **clamp connections**. They count as a typical feature of the group.

The cells of the long-lived mycelium mostly have two different cell nuclei. This is called **dikaryotic**, or having paired nuclei. The two nuclei stay separate for a long time. Only in the **young basidium** do they fuse into one nucleus. This nucleus then divides, and in this way the spores arise. With the spores, the fungi can reproduce and spread.

The basidiomycetes include many **edible mushrooms**: **porcini**, chanterelle and button mushroom. The poisonous fly agaric also belongs here. Many basidiomycetes live together with trees or break down wood and leaves. Some, however, are **plant pathogens**: **rust fungi** and **smut fungi** attack cereals and other crop plants and can cause great harvest losses.

gewusst: A single mushroom with a cap can release billions of spores.
A honey fungus mycelium can spread underground over a huge area and is among the largest living things on Earth.

teile.einleitung: In summer, meadows, fields and gardens bloom in all colours. Some summer flowers grow wild, others we plant in the garden. You probably know many of them already.
wichtigste: Young sunflowers turn to follow the Sun during the day.
The red corn poppy likes to grow at the edge of cornfields.
The blue cornflower gets its name from the grain, the corn.
In the Alps, deep blue gentian and pink alpenroses bloom.
Lavender has a strong scent and is put in scent sachets.
An ointment for the skin is made from the marigold.

abschnitte.text: The **sunflower** is tall and bright yellow. Young plants turn their heads during the day with the Sun from east to west. When fully grown, their flowers mostly face east. In the middle many seeds ripen. Birds like to eat them, and oil is also made from them.

abschnitte.titel: Flowers at the edge of the field
abschnitte.text: The **corn poppy** has thin, bright red petals. It likes to grow at field edges and on fallow land. The **cornflower** blooms bright blue. In the past it often grew among the grain, that is, in the corn. That is how it got its name.

In mountain meadows the **gentian** blooms deep blue. Its flowers look like small bells or funnels. The **alpenrose** is a small shrub. In June and July it colours whole slopes pink in the Swiss Alps.

The **nasturtium** blooms orange, yellow or red all summer. Its flowers and leaves taste peppery and even go into salad. **Lavender** blooms violet and has a strong scent. Its dried flowers are put in scent sachets. The orange **marigold** blooms from June into autumn. From its flowers a healing ointment for the skin is made.

gewusst: Bees, bumblebees and butterflies find plenty of nectar on summer flowers.
Some flowers can be eaten, for example the flowers of the nasturtium.

teile.einleitung: Yarrow is a common meadow flower with white flowers and finely feathered leaves. It smells spicy and has long been used as a medicinal herb.
wichtigste: Yarrow mostly blooms white, sometimes pale pink.
Its leaves are finely divided like little feathers.
Many small flower heads form a flat disc at the top.
When crushed, it smells strongly spicy.
Its Latin name “Achillea” recalls the hero Achilles.
It survives dry weather very well.

abschnitte.text: **Yarrow** mostly blooms **white**, sometimes pale pink. What looks like a flower is a small **flower head** made of many tiny flowers. Many of these heads sit together and form a flat, umbrella-like **disc** at the top. Yarrow belongs to the **daisy family**, like the daisy.

The leaves of yarrow are very finely divided. They look like small green **feathers**. The scientific name is “Achillea millefolium”. “Millefolium” means “thousand leaves”, because each leaf has so many fine lobes. If you crush a leaf, it smells strongly **spicy** and a little bitter, because the plant contains **fragrant oils**.

The German name of yarrow, “Schafgarbe”, contains the word for **sheep**, “Schaf”. It is said that sheep like to eat the plant. The Latin name “Achillea” recalls **Achilles**, a hero from an old Greek legend. According to the legend, he is supposed to have treated wounds with the plant.

**Tea** has been made from yarrow for a very long time. It is said to help with **stomach ache**, for example. Yarrow is very tough. It grows in meadows, on dry **verges** and on banks. It also survives long dry weather well. In Switzerland you find it from the lowlands up into the high mountains.

gewusst: A single flower head of yarrow consists of several tiny individual flowers.
Many insects such as beetles and hoverflies visit the flat flower discs.

teile.einleitung: Ferns, mosses and fungi do not form seeds. They reproduce with tiny spores. Spores are so small and light that the wind can carry them far.
wichtigste: Spores are tiny, as small as a speck of dust.
They are mostly spread by the wind.
A single fern produces a great many spores, often millions.
Spores need a damp place to germinate.
From a fern spore, a tiny green plate, the prothallus, grows first.
The button mushroom forms its spores on the gills under the cap.

abschnitte.text: A **spore** is as small as a **speck of dust**. Without a microscope you can hardly see a single spore. Because spores are so light, the **wind** carries them far away. In this way they reach new places. A fern produces huge numbers of them, often **millions**.

Under a fern frond you often see small clusters. In them the spores form. When they are ripe, the clusters are usually **brown**, and the spores fall out. If a spore lands in a good place, a tiny, heart-shaped, green plate grows from it first. It is called a **prothallus**. Only from this does a new fern develop later.

Spores germinate only if they lie **damp** enough. That is why ferns and **mosses** often grow in damp, shady places. Only very few of the many spores land in a good place. That is why the plant makes so many of them.

**Fungi** also form spores. In the **button mushroom**, thin plates sit under the cap, the **gills**. The spores form there. Funny is the **puffball**: if you press on a ripe puffball, millions of brown spores puff out like a cloud of smoke.

gewusst: A single puffball cloud can consist of millions of spores.
Spores float so lightly that some are even carried over mountains and seas.

teile.einleitung: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is a vault for seeds in the far north. It lies deep inside a mountain on Spitsbergen and keeps backup copies of seeds from all over the world. If something is lost in a gene bank, it can be fetched back from here.
wichtigste: The seed vault lies near Longyearbyen on Spitsbergen, which belongs to Norway.
It was opened on 26 February 2008.
The seeds are stored at about minus 18 degrees Celsius.
The vault has room for 4.5 million seed samples.
The seeds continue to belong to the gene banks that deposit them.
In 2015 the research centre ICARDA was the first to take seeds back.

abschnitte.text: The vault lies near **Longyearbyen** on the island group of **Spitsbergen**, which belongs to Norway. A long tunnel leads into a mountain. There the storage chambers lie in the **permafrost**, that is, in ground that is frozen all year round. Cooling systems keep the rooms at about minus 18 degrees Celsius. Even if the power fails, it stays below zero thanks to the permafrost.

All over the world there are **gene banks** that keep seeds of crop plants. They secure old varieties of wheat, rice, beans and many other plants. But gene banks can be destroyed by war, accidents or natural disasters. That is why they send **backup copies** to Spitsbergen. The vault is like an insurance policy for the food supply of humankind.

The vault works on the principle of a **black box**. The seeds arrive in sealed boxes, and nobody except the depositing gene bank may open them. The seeds therefore continue to belong to the gene banks. The vault is built for **4.5 million samples**. At up to 500 seeds per sample, that would be over two billion seeds.

In 2015, a gene bank took seeds back for the first time. The research centre **ICARDA** could no longer use its gene bank near Aleppo because of the civil war in Syria. With the copies from Spitsbergen, it rebuilt its collections in Lebanon and Morocco. In autumn 2016, after warm, rainy weather, **meltwater** got into the access tunnel. The seeds stayed undamaged, and the entrance was later renewed.

gewusst: In the cold of the vault, many seeds stay able to germinate for decades, some probably much longer.
The vault is often called the “doomsday vault”, because it is meant to survive even great catastrophes.

teile.einleitung: Spore plants form no flowers and no seeds. They reproduce with tiny spores. They include mosses, ferns, horsetails and club mosses, the oldest land plants on Earth.
wichtigste: Plants without flowers that reproduce with spores are called cryptogams.
A spore usually consists of only one cell, while a seed contains an embryo and nutritive tissue.
Ferns, horsetails and club mosses together form the pteridophytes.
Conifers are not spore plants but seed plants.
The first land plants, over 400 million years ago, were moss-like spore plants.
The spore wall consists of the very durable substance sporopollenin.

abschnitte.text: Spore plants form no flowers. With a technical term they are called **cryptogams**. The word comes from Greek, and “kryptos” means hidden. In the past, people could not see how they reproduce. Plants with flowers, by contrast, are called **phanerogams** or seed plants.

A **seed** contains a small embryo and nutritive tissue as a store. A **spore** is usually only a single cell with a protective wall. This wall consists of **sporopollenin**, one of the most durable natural substances of all. That is why spores can still be found in rocks even after millions of years.

The spore plants include the **mosses** and the **pteridophytes**. Pteridophytes are ferns, **horsetails** and **club mosses**. Unlike the mosses, they have vascular bundles, that is, fine tubes for water. The **stag’s-horn clubmoss** forms shoots metres long that creep along the ground with small leaves. Club mosses are protected in many areas. **Conifers** do not belong, because they form seeds in cones.

The first plants on dry land were moss-like **spore plants**. They appeared in the Palaeozoic **over 400 million years ago**. Later, giant horsetails and club mosses grew into whole forests. From their remains, **hard coal** formed in many places. Flowering plants appeared only much later.

**Fungi** also form spores. In the past they were therefore counted among the plants. But fungi have no **chlorophyll** and feed on other substances. That is why they now form a **kingdom of their own** alongside plants and animals.

gewusst: Much hard coal comes from giant club mosses and horsetails that grew millions of years ago.
Spores are so resistant that researchers can still tell from ancient rocks which plants grew at that time.

teile.einleitung: The sunflower is a large plant with bright yellow petals and a huge flower head. Oil is obtained from its seeds, and people and birds like to nibble them. Young sunflowers even turn their heads with the Sun during the day.
wichtigste: Sunflowers have yellow petals and a large flower head.
The head consists of hundreds to thousands of small individual flowers.
The sunflower originally comes from North and Central America.
Young sunflowers turn their heads towards the Sun during the day.
Sunflower oil is made from the seeds.
People and birds like to eat the seeds.
Sunflowers can grow over three metres tall.

abschnitte.text: The sunflower belongs to the **daisy family**, like the daisy. What looks like a single flower is in truth a head made of many small flowers. On the outside sit yellow **ray florets** that look like petals. On the inside lie brown disc florets, from which the seeds later develop.

The sunflower originally comes from North America and Mexico. Indigenous peoples grew it there over 4,000 years ago. Spanish seafarers brought it to Europe in the 16th century. Today it is grown in large quantities mainly in Russia, Ukraine and Argentina.

Young sunflowers turn their heads during the day with the Sun from east to west. At night they swing back to the east. This movement is called **heliotropism**. Fully grown, flowering sunflowers, by contrast, usually stay facing east.

The seeds are actually fruits with a seed inside. From them **sunflower oil** is pressed, one of the most important cooking oils in the world. Shelled seeds go into bread, muesli and salads. Birds such as tits and finches love sunflower seeds, which is why they are in **bird food** in winter.

In Switzerland, too, sunflowers are grown in fields, mainly in Vaud and on the Central Plateau. In summer whole fields glow yellow there. Many farms offer fields for **pick-your-own**. In the garden sunflowers are popular because they grow fast and attract bees.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family whose flower consists of many small individual flowers.
When a plant turns towards the Sun.
The yellow flowers at the edge that look like petals.
Oil that is used for cooking and eating.

gewusst: The seeds in the flower head are arranged in spirals that follow a mathematical pattern.
The sunflower is the national flower of Ukraine.
The painter Vincent van Gogh painted several famous pictures of sunflowers.

teile.einleitung: Teosinte is a wild grass from Mexico and Central America. About 9000 years ago, people bred maize from it. Although the two are closely related, they hardly look alike.
wichtigste: Maize descends from teosinte.
It was domesticated in the south of what is now Mexico.
The closest wild form grows in the Balsas River valley.
Domestication began about 9000 years ago.
Teosinte kernels are enclosed in a hard casing.
An ear of teosinte bears only about 5 to 12 kernels.

abschnitte.text: Genetic studies show that **maize** came from a subspecies of **teosinte**. This subspecies is called Zea mays parviglumis and grows in the valley of the **Río Balsas** in Mexico. Very old traces of maize were found there too. Maize and teosinte are so closely related that they can be crossed. Even so, they look very different.

**Domestication** means that people breed a wild plant over many generations into a crop. With maize this happened in the south of what is now **Mexico**. Genetic dating and finds of starch grains point to a start about **9000 years ago**. Large cobs only appeared over thousands of years. From Mexico, maize spread across the whole of the Americas.

An ear of teosinte consists of only about **5 to 12 kernels** lying one behind the other. A modern maize cob, on the other hand, bears several hundred kernels. Teosinte kernels are enclosed in a **hard fruit casing**. A change in the gene **tga1** exposed the kernel in maize. Another gene, **tb1**, makes sure that maize forms one main stem instead of many side shoots.

For a long time it was unclear where maize came from. The geneticist **George Beadle**, later a Nobel Prize winner, put forward the teosinte hypothesis early on. He studied teosinte and crossed it with maize. Other researchers had other ideas. Only genetic studies confirmed Beadle’s assumption.

gewusst: Teosinte is heavily branched and forms many side shoots, whereas maize mostly has just one strong main stem.
Today maize is one of the most widely grown crops in the world, even though its wild form has only tiny ears.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine is the only national park in Switzerland. Here nature may develop freely, and humans are only guests. That is why strict rules apply.
wichtigste: Switzerland has a single national park with this strict protection.
It lies in the Engadine in the canton of Graubünden and was founded in 1914.
Visitors must not leave the paths.
Dogs are not allowed in the park, not even on a lead.
Camping is forbidden.
Ibex, marmots and reintroduced bearded vultures live in the park.

abschnitte.titel: The oldest national park in the Alps
abschnitte.text: The Swiss National Park was founded in **1914** and is the oldest national park in the Alps. It lies in the **Lower Engadine** in the canton of **Graubünden**, around the Ofen Pass. The visitor centre is in **Zernez**. The landscape ranges from mountain forests and alpine pastures to rocks and scree. Since the founding, no hunting, felling or mowing has taken place here.

In the national park, nature comes first. That is why you must **not leave the marked paths**. **Dogs** are not allowed at all, because they could disturb wild animals. **Camping**, making fires and sleeping in the open are forbidden. Picking plants, taking stones away or feeding animals is also not allowed. You can stay overnight in a hotel or a hut in the park.

The **ibex** with its large, curved horns was once wiped out in Switzerland. From 1920 it was reintroduced in the national park. Today you often see it on steep slopes. The **marmot** lives in burrows on alpine pastures. If danger threatens, for example from an eagle, it lets out a loud **whistle**, and all disappear into the burrow.

abschnitte.titel: The return of the bearded vulture
abschnitte.text: The **bearded vulture** is one of the largest birds of the Alps. Over a hundred years ago it had disappeared from the Alps. From **1991**, young bearded vultures were released in the national park. Since then bearded vultures breed in Switzerland again. The bearded vulture eats mainly the bones of dead animals, which it sometimes drops from the air onto rocks so that they break.

abschnitte.titel: A laboratory under the open sky
abschnitte.text: Because nature in the park develops without interference, it is very valuable for **research**. Scientists have been observing for decades how forests, meadows and animal populations change. **Red deer**, chamois, foxes and many species of birds also live in the park.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park belongs to the strictest protection category for natural areas of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the IUCN.
The bearded vulture can digest bones so large that it swallows them almost whole.

teile.einleitung: Solanine is a natural poison that potatoes and other members of the nightshade family make. It protects the plant from herbivores. Anyone who knows where solanine is found can still enjoy potatoes without worry.
wichtigste: Solanine is a glycoalkaloid, that is, an alkaloid with sugar building blocks attached.
Most solanine is in and directly under the skin and in the eyes.
Green spots and sprouts of the potato must be cut away generously.
Cooking hardly destroys solanine.
The green berries of the potato plant are poisonous and must never be eaten.
Too much solanine causes stomach ache, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

abschnitte.text: The potato belongs to the genus **Solanum**, the nightshades. **Solanine** is named after this genus. Chemically it is an **alkaloid** to which sugar building blocks are attached. That is why it is also called a **glycoalkaloid**. The plant uses it to protect itself from animals and diseases.

In a potato tuber, most solanine lies in the **skin**, in the layer directly beneath it and in the **eyes**. Sprouts and green spots also contain a lot of it. Peeling and cutting away green spots greatly lower the content. Especially poisonous are the small **green berries** that grow on the plant after flowering. They look like mini tomatoes and must never be eaten.

Solanine withstands high temperatures well. In cooking it is therefore **hardly destroyed**. A green potato does not become safe by cooking. You have to cut away the green parts generously beforehand. Potatoes that are very green or have sprouted heavily are better thrown away.

Solanine irritates the **stomach and gut**. Anyone who eats too much of it gets stomach pains, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Normal, well-stored potatoes contain only very little solanine. Children are more sensitive than adults, so caution is especially worthwhile.

**Light** and **warmth** make potatoes turn green and sprout. That is why you store them **dark and cool**, for example in the cellar. The **tomato** is also a member of the nightshade family. Unripe, green tomatoes contain similar poisonous substances, which are broken down as they ripen.

gewusst: The green of a potato is chlorophyll and itself not poisonous, but it shows that more solanine has usually formed there too.
The berries of the potato plant look harmless like small tomatoes but are strongly poisonous.

teile.einleitung: The snowdrop is one of the very first spring flowers. Often it is already blooming while snow still lies. Its white flowers hang downwards like little bells.
wichtigste: The snowdrop has white flowers like little bells.
It mostly blooms in February and March.
It grows from a bulb every year.
The flower has six petals, and the inner ones carry a green spot.
All parts are poisonous, especially the bulb.
Bees find food here as early as February.

abschnitte.text: The **snowdrop** has **white** flowers. They look like little **bells**. Each flower has **six** petals: three long outer ones and three short inner ones. The inner petals carry a **green spot**. The outer ones have no spot.

The snowdrop blooms very early in the year, mostly in **February** and **March**. Often it is still blooming among remnants of snow. That is why it is called snowdrop. The flower **nods downwards**. In this way the pollen stays dry in rain and snow.

In the ground the snowdrop has a small **bulb**. In it, **food** is stored for the next year. That is why it can sprout so early, when it is still cold. In early summer the leaves wither, and the plant rests in the ground until the next winter. In time new bulbs form, and small groups develop.

On warm days, the first **bees** fly out as early as February. They collect **pollen** from snowdrops. For people, however, snowdrops are **poisonous**, all parts and especially the bulb. You may look at them, but not eat them. Ants carry the seeds away and in this way help to spread the plant.

gewusst: Snowdrops can push their way up through thin layers of snow.
In gardens and parks there are often huge carpets of snowdrops.

teile.einleitung: The coneflower is a colourful flower that blooms in many gardens. The middle of its flower rises up like a small hat. Bees and butterflies like to visit it very much.
wichtigste: The middle of the flower looks like a small hat.
The coneflower comes from North America.
The purple coneflower blooms pink to purple, the yellow coneflower golden yellow with a dark centre.
The coneflower is a perennial and comes back every year.
It loves a sunny spot.
Drops and tea are made from the purple coneflower.

abschnitte.text: The **coneflower** has a special flower. Its middle rises up and recalls a **small hat**. All around stand the coloured petals. As its German name, “Sonnenhut”, or sun hat, says, it loves the **sun**. In a bright spot it blooms lushly in summer and autumn.

There are different coneflowers. The **purple coneflower**, called “Roter Sonnenhut”, or red coneflower, in German, actually blooms **pink to purple**. Its centre is orange-brown. The **yellow coneflower** has golden yellow petals and an almost black centre. Both are popular garden flowers.

The coneflower grows wild in meadows in **North America**. Today it stands in many Swiss gardens. It is a **perennial**. That means that in winter it rests in the ground, and in spring it sprouts anew. In this way it comes back every year.

abschnitte.titel: Food for insects and a medicinal plant
abschnitte.text: The coneflower has a lot of **nectar** and pollen. That is why bees, bumblebees and **butterflies** like to fly to it. From the purple coneflower, drops and tea are also made. They are used, for example, for **colds**. So it is also a **medicinal plant**.

gewusst: If you leave the faded heads standing in winter, birds can still find seeds in them.
The scientific name of the purple coneflower is Echinacea, which is also what many remedies made from it are called.

teile.einleitung: Ribwort plantain is one of the most common plants in Swiss meadows and at the edges of paths. You recognise it by its long, narrow leaves. It has long been used as a home remedy against coughs and mosquito bites.
wichtigste: The leaves are long, narrow and pointed like a lance.
The leaf veins run almost parallel along the length.
The flower head is a brownish spike on a long, leafless stalk.
Ribwort plantain grows in meadows, pastures and at the edges of paths and tolerates trampling well.
As tea or syrup it is a well-known home remedy for coughs.
A crushed leaf relieves the itching of mosquito bites.

abschnitte.text: **Ribwort plantain** has long, narrow, pointed leaves. Its Latin name **“lanceolata”** means lance-shaped. Several strong **leaf veins** run almost parallel from the base to the tip. If you tear off a leaf, you can see these fibres clearly. The leaves form a rosette on the ground.

The tiny flowers sit densely in a brownish **spike** on a long, leafless stalk. The pale stamens stick out like a wreath. Ribwort plantain is very common. It grows in **meadows**, pastures and at **path edges** and tolerates being walked on well.

Ribwort plantain contains **mucilage**. It swells with water and forms a protective film. As **tea** or **syrup**, it lies soothingly on the irritated throat. That is why it is a well-known **home remedy for coughs**.

When out and about, you can crush a leaf and lay it on a **mosquito bite**. The juice cools and relieves the itching. This also helps after a nettle sting. That is why ribwort plantain is also called the **plaster of the meadow**.

In the same genus is the **greater plantain**. It has broad, rounded leaves. Often it grows directly on trampled paths. That is also where the German name “Wegerich” comes from, which has “Weg”, or path, in it.

gewusst: Ribwort plantain grows almost everywhere in Switzerland, from the lowlands up into the mountains.
The parallel fibres are so tough that when you tear off a leaf they hang out like threads.

teile.einleitung: The thermohaline circulation is a gigantic ocean current that links all the world’s oceans with each other. It is driven by differences in the temperature and salt content of the water. It is also called the global conveyor belt of the oceans.
wichtigste: The thermohaline circulation is a worldwide system of ocean currents.
Thermo means heat and haline means salt.
Cold, salty water is heavier and sinks into the depths.
It carries heat and salt water over great distances and influences the climate of whole continents.
The Gulf Stream is also linked to this system and brings warmth to Europe.
One complete circuit takes about 1000 years.
Researchers fear that climate change is weakening the current in the Atlantic.

abschnitte.text: The word **thermohaline** is put together from the Greek words for heat and salt. It describes ocean currents that arise because water is of different weights. Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water. Heavy water sinks downwards, lighter water rises, and that is how the sea is set in motion.

In the North Atlantic near Greenland, warm surface water cools down strongly in winter. When **sea ice** forms, the salt stays behind in the water, and the sea water becomes even saltier. This cold, salty water is very heavy and sinks to a depth of several thousand metres. Around Antarctica, too, this kind of **deep water** sinks down.

The water that has sunk flows slowly south along the sea floor and spreads into the Indian and Pacific Oceans. There it gradually rises to the surface again and warms up. As a surface current it finally returns to the Atlantic. This cycle is compared to a **conveyor belt** that takes about 1000 years for one circuit.

abschnitte.titel: The Gulf Stream and Europe’s climate
abschnitte.text: The **Gulf Stream** flows out of the Gulf of Mexico along the coast of North America and across the Atlantic. Its continuation, the North Atlantic Current, brings warm water as far as Norway. That is why it is much milder in Western Europe than in Canada at the same latitude. The weather in Switzerland also benefits from this heat pump of the ocean.

Because of global warming, the ice on Greenland is melting, and a lot of fresh water flows into the North Atlantic. As a result, the sea water there becomes lighter and does not sink as well. Measurements suggest that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or **AMOC** for short, is weakening. A strong slowdown could change the climate in Europe and the rainy seasons in other parts of the world.

The current brings oxygen from the surface into the deep sea, where otherwise hardly any life would be possible. Where nutrient-rich deep water rises again, many fish thrive. The oceans also store a great deal of heat and carbon dioxide. This means the thermohaline circulation plays a key role in the Earth’s **climate system**.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a substance is in relation to its size
How much salt is dissolved in sea water
Cold, heavy water that flows in the depths of the sea
Short for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which includes the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current

gewusst: A drop of water that sinks into the depths near Greenland today will only come back to the surface in about 1000 years.
The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the rivers of the Earth put together.
In the film “The Day After Tomorrow” the current stops within a few days, but in reality it would take much longer.

teile.einleitung: Woodpeckers are birds that hack into wood with their strong beak. You often hear them before you see them. In Swiss forests and gardens, several species of woodpecker live.
wichtigste: Woodpeckers hack with the beak for food and carve holes in wood.
With their very long tongue they pull larvae out of narrow tunnels.
The great spotted woodpecker is the most common woodpecker in Switzerland.
The black woodpecker is the largest woodpecker in Europe.
The green woodpecker searches on the ground for ants.
In spring, woodpeckers drum to show their territory.

abschnitte.text: Woodpeckers search in the wood for **larvae** and other insects. For this they hack with their strong **beak**. They also carve **holes** in which they raise their young. With their feet they cling to the bark. Their hard, stiff **tail feathers** they brace against the trunk like a prop.

Woodpeckers have a very **long tongue**. At its tip sit small barbs. With them they pull larvae out of their tunnels in the wood. At rest the long tongue lies folded up in the head. In this way the woodpecker can reach food even in deep, narrow holes.

The **great spotted woodpecker** is coloured black, white and red. It is the most common here and occurs in almost every forest and even in gardens. The **black woodpecker** is almost as big as a crow, entirely black and has a red cap. It is the largest woodpecker in Europe. The **green woodpecker** has green plumage. It often searches on the ground and pokes in meadows for **ants**.
In spring, woodpeckers drum fast and loud on branches. This can be heard from far away. With it they show other woodpeckers: this is my **territory**. So drumming is a kind of song without a voice.

Many woodpeckers like to build new holes. The old ones stay behind in the tree. Other animals move into them, for example **tits**, owls or **bats**. Woodpeckers are therefore important for many forest dwellers. Old trees with holes are thus valuable for nature.

gewusst: The woodpecker’s head is built so that it can withstand the many hard blows well.
Without woodpeckers, many birds and bats in the forest would have no home.

teile.einleitung: Saxifrage is a plant genus that often grows in rock crevices and in stony places. Many species live in the Alps, some even right up in the eternal ice.
wichtigste: Saxifrage often grows in rock crevices.
The name comes from the way the plant seems to break stones.
Worldwide there are several hundred species of saxifrage.
Many species have leaves in a round rosette.
The purple saxifrage blooms pink to violet and forms flat cushions.
It was found on the Dom at 4505 metres, as high as no other flowering plant in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Saxifrage likes to grow where other plants can hardly find room: in **rock crevices**, on scree and on walls. Its roots penetrate fine cracks in the stone. That is why it looks as if the plant were breaking the stone. This is also where the name comes from, since saxifrage means **stone breaker**. In the world there are **several hundred** species, many of them in mountains.

In many species of saxifrage, the leaves are arranged in a round **rosette**, close to the ground. In this way they are well protected from wind and cold. Other species form flat **cushions** that lie on the rock like small pillows. In a cushion it stays warmer and moister than in the surroundings. This helps in the harsh mountain climate.
