The **livelong saxifrage** has a rosette of firm leaves. On the leaf edge you see **white specks of lime**. They arise because the plant gives off water there in which lime is dissolved. When the water evaporates, the lime stays behind. In summer a stem with many small white flowers grows from the rosette.

The **purple saxifrage** forms flat cushions and blooms **pink to violet**. It is one of the first flowers to bloom in the mountains after the snow melts. It tolerates cold, wind and strong sun. In Switzerland it was found on the **Dom** in the Valais at **4505 metres**. No other flowering plant has been found higher in Switzerland.

gewusst: The purple saxifrage also grows in the Arctic, far to the north.
Many species of saxifrage are planted in rock gardens.

teile.einleitung: The subalpine zone is the altitude zone directly below the treeline. The uppermost forests of the Alps grow here, and the climate is already harsh and cool.
wichtigste: The subalpine zone lies directly below the treeline.
The prefix “sub” means “under”.
In the northern Alps, spruce forms most of the forests here.
The growing season is much shorter than on the Central Plateau.
Spruces have narrow, pointed crowns so that snow slides off more easily.
Many trees stand in small, dense groups called clumps.

abschnitte.text: The Alps are divided into **altitude zones**. Above the montane zone comes the **subalpine zone**. It lies **directly below the treeline**. The prefix **“sub”** means **“under”**, so subalpine means “below the alpine zone”. Above it begin the treeless alpine pastures. In the Swiss Alps, the subalpine zone lies roughly between 1600 and 2000 metres, somewhat higher or lower depending on the region.

In the subalpine zone of the northern Alps, **spruce** forms most of the forests. In the drier central Alps, for example in the Valais and the Engadine, many **larches** and **Swiss stone pines** grow. The spruces here often have **narrow, pointed crowns**. In this way **snow slides off more easily**, and the branches do not break. The trees often stand in small, dense groups, the **clumps**.

The climate is cool, the winter long and snowy. The **growing season** is **much shorter** than on the Central Plateau. Trees therefore grow slowly. Beneath the trees, dwarf shrubs such as **alpenrose** and **bilberry** thrive. The forests protect villages and roads in the valley from avalanches and rockfall. That is why many of them are **protection forests**.

Farmers have used this zone for a long time. Between valley and alp there are often the **mid-mountain pastures**. These are pastures with small huts that are used in spring and autumn. In light conifer forests of the montane and subalpine zones lives the **capercaillie**, a large, rare grouse. Black grouse, nutcrackers and chamois are also at home here.

gewusst: The nutcracker hides stone pine seeds and so helps new stone pines to grow.
A Swiss stone pine can live to be several hundred years old.

teile.einleitung: A snow cover is more than just cold whiteness. It acts like a warm blanket for the ground, for plants and for small animals. In the mountains it decides how long the summer lasts for plants.
wichtigste: Fresh powder snow consists of over 90 per cent air.
Under a thick snow cover the ground stays at around 0 degrees.
Without snow, the ground freezes deep in cold winters.
In winter, mice live in the subnivean space under the snow.
The rock ptarmigan digs itself into the snow on cold nights.
If the snow melts early, late frosts can damage young shoots.

abschnitte.text: Fresh **powder snow** consists of over 90 per cent trapped **air**. Air conducts heat badly. That is why snow **insulates** very well. Under a deep snow cover the ground usually stays **at around 0 degrees**, even when it is much colder above. The snow cover holds back the warmth of the ground and shields it from the cold air.

Between the ground and the snow cover lies the **subnivean space**. It is dark there, but steadily cool and windless. **Mice** and other small mammals stay active here all winter. They make **tunnels** and find food. Many plants also spend the winter green under the snow.

The **rock ptarmigan** uses the snow cover as protection. On very cold winter nights it **digs itself into the snow**. In the snow hole it is much warmer than on the surface. In this way it saves valuable energy. In winter its plumage is white, so it is well camouflaged in the snow.

In the mountains there are **hollows** where snow stays especially long. They are called **snow beds**. The snow-free period there often lasts only a few weeks. A plant community of its own grows here, adapted to short summers. Typical is the **herbaceous willow**. It grows only a few centimetres tall and is regarded as one of the smallest trees in the world.

In cold winters with **little snow**, the frost penetrates deep into the ground. This can damage roots and soil organisms. If the snow melts in spring **earlier** than usual, young shoots and buds are directly exposed to **late frosts**. This can seriously damage alpine plants. In Switzerland, the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos studies the snow cover.

gewusst: A snow hole can protect people from cold and wind in an emergency.
No two snow crystals are exactly alike.

teile.einleitung: A savanna is a wide grassland with scattered trees and shrubs. It is found in warm regions of the Earth, and the best known are the savannas of Africa. Many large animals live there.
wichtigste: Mostly grass with scattered trees grows in the savanna.
There is a rainy season and a dry season.
Typical trees are the umbrella thorn acacia and the baobab.
Giraffes, zebras, elephants and ostriches live in the African savanna.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal.
The African elephant is the largest land animal.

abschnitte.text: In the **savanna**, mostly tall **grass** grows. Between it stand scattered trees and shrubs. Savannas are found in Africa, South America, India and Australia. It is warm all year round. A famous area is the **Serengeti** in East Africa.

In the savanna a **rainy season** and a **dry season** alternate. In the rainy season everything turns green and there is plenty of food. In the dry season the grass turns yellow and parched. Many animals then travel long distances to find water and fresh grass.

The **umbrella thorn acacia** has a broad, flat crown like an umbrella. Giraffes like to eat its leaves. The **baobab**, which in German is called the “monkey bread tree”, has a very thick trunk. In it, it stores water for the dry season. In this way both trees survive long months without rain.

With its long neck, the **giraffe** reaches leaves high up in the trees. **Zebras** with their black and white stripes live in **herds**. The **African elephant** is the largest animal that lives on land. The **ostrich** is the largest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but it can run very fast.

Predators such as lions, hyenas and cheetahs also live in the savanna. The **cheetah** is the **fastest land animal**. For a short time it can run at over 90 kilometres per hour. But it cannot keep up this speed for long. That is why it first creeps up close to its prey.

gewusst: Every zebra has its own stripe pattern, and no two are exactly alike.
Baobabs can live to be many hundreds of years old.

teile.einleitung: Succulents are plants that store water in thick leaves, stems or roots. In this way they survive long periods without rain. They include cacti, aloe vera and also the houseleek from the Alps.
wichtigste: Succulents store water in their juicy tissue.
The cactus is the best known succulent.
In many cacti, the leaves have been modified into spines.
Almost all cacti originally come from the Americas.
The saguaro is a giant columnar cactus from the deserts of the USA and Mexico.
The houseleek also grows in Switzerland on sunny rocks.
Indoors, succulents are watered only rarely.

abschnitte.text: The word **succulent** comes from the Latin word for “juicy”. These plants have a thick tissue that fills with water like a sponge. Some store the water in the leaves, and they are called **leaf succulents**. Others, such as the cacti, store it in the stem. In this way they can survive weeks or even months without rain.

Cacti are the best known succulents. In many of them, the leaves have turned into **spines**. Spines lose hardly any water and protect the plant from thirsty animals. The green work of the leaves is taken over by the thick stem. Almost all cacti come from the **Americas**, above all from Mexico and the USA. Only humans brought them to other parts of the world.

The **saguaro** is a mighty columnar cactus from the deserts of the south-west of the USA and in Mexico. It can grow over twelve metres tall, growing very slowly as it does so. After rain it soaks itself full of water and becomes thicker. Its ribs work like a concertina that can expand. Birds often build holes in its trunk.

There are succulents in Switzerland too. The **houseleek** forms thick leaf rosettes and grows on dry, sunny rocks, also in the Alps. The **biting stonecrop** grows on walls and roofs. Both manage with very little soil and water. In the past, people liked to plant houseleek on roofs, because according to old folk belief it was supposed to protect against lightning.

Many people keep succulents as house plants, for example **aloe vera**. Its thick leaves contain a gel that is used in skin creams. Succulents need a lot of light but little water. You water them only when the soil is completely dry. Too much water makes the **roots rot**, and the plant dies.

gewusst: Many succulents open their stomata only in the cool night, so that they lose hardly any water on the hot day.
Some spurges from Africa look so like cacti that they are easy to confuse, although they are not related to them at all.
The English name houseleek comes from the way the plant was often grown on house roofs.

teile.einleitung: The nitrogen cycle describes how the element nitrogen travels to and fro between air, soil, living things and water. Nitrogen is an important building block for the proteins and genetic material of all living things. Although air is about 78 per cent nitrogen, most living things cannot use it directly.
wichtigste: Dry air consists of about 78 per cent nitrogen.
Only certain bacteria can bind atmospheric nitrogen with the enzyme nitrogenase.
Plants take up nitrogen mainly as nitrate and ammonium.
In nitrification, bacteria convert ammonium via nitrite into nitrate.
In denitrification, nitrate is turned back into atmospheric nitrogen when oxygen is lacking.
With the Haber-Bosch process, ammonia is made for artificial fertiliser.
Too much fertiliser burdens waters and produces the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide.

abschnitte.text: Dry air consists of roughly **78 per cent** nitrogen in the form of N2. In this molecule, two nitrogen atoms are joined by a very firm triple bond. That is why N2 is very unreactive. Plants and animals cannot use this nitrogen directly, although they urgently need it for **proteins** and DNA.

Certain bacteria can crack the firm atmospheric nitrogen. They use the enzyme **nitrogenase** for this and convert N2 into ammonia. Some of these bacteria, the rhizobia, live in nodules on the roots of legumes such as clover, beans and peas. Lightning also converts a small amount of atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen compounds.

abschnitte.titel: From the soil into the plant
abschnitte.text: When plants and animals die, bacteria and fungi break them down, and **ammonium** is produced. In **nitrification**, bacteria such as Nitrosomonas convert ammonium into nitrite. Bacteria of the genus Nitrobacter then oxidise the nitrite to nitrate. Plants take up nitrogen mainly as nitrate and ammonium through their roots, and animals get it through their food.

In wet soils, swamps and waters, there is often little oxygen. There, bacteria convert nitrate back into gaseous nitrogen N2. This process is called **denitrification**. This closes the cycle, and the nitrogen returns to the atmosphere.

At the beginning of the 20th century, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed the **Haber-Bosch process**. With it, ammonia is made from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen, the raw material for artificial fertiliser. Thanks to this invention, many more people can be fed today. At the same time, humans have greatly increased the amount of bound nitrogen on Earth.

Too much fertiliser and slurry reach the groundwater, streams and lakes. There they promote the growth of algae, and nitrate can burden drinking water. From fertilised soils, the greenhouse gas **nitrous oxide**, also called laughing gas, escapes. In Switzerland, large parts of the nitrogen load come from agriculture, especially from ammonia from livestock farming.

begriffe.erklaerung: Converting atmospheric nitrogen into compounds that living things can use.
Bacteria convert ammonium via nitrite into nitrate.
Bacteria turn nitrate back into atmospheric nitrogen.
A nitrogen compound that plants take up as a nutrient.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in living things.

gewusst: Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch each received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
About half of the nitrogen in our body today comes from artificial fertiliser made by the Haber-Bosch process.
Nitrous oxide acts about 300 times more strongly as a greenhouse gas than the same amount of CO2.

teile.einleitung: Butterflies are insects that fly by day. They visit flowers, bask on stones and often have beautifully coloured wings. Before a butterfly flies, it was an egg, a caterpillar and a chrysalis.
wichtigste: Butterflies warm up in the sun in the morning.
A caterpillar hatches from the egg.
The caterpillar pupates and becomes a butterfly in the chrysalis.
The wings are covered with tiny scales.
Butterflies taste with their feet.
The brimstone flies as early as February or March.

abschnitte.text: A butterfly changes greatly in its life. A **caterpillar** hatches from the **egg**. It eats a lot and moults several times, because it grows. Then it becomes a **chrysalis**. In the chrysalis it transforms into a butterfly. This transformation is called **metamorphosis**.

Butterflies are cold-blooded, and their body is as warm as their surroundings. In the morning they therefore need **warmth from the sun** before they can fly well. Often they sit in the sun with open wings. With their long **proboscis** they suck nectar from flowers. At rest, the proboscis is rolled up like a watch spring.

The wings of butterflies are covered with tiny **scales**. They lie one over another like roof tiles and give the wings their colours. If you touch a butterfly, the fine dust stays on your fingers. That is why you should not touch butterflies. With their **feet** they taste whether a leaf is right for their eggs.

The **brimstone** is bright yellow and overwinters as a butterfly. On warm days in February or March it is already flying. The **peacock butterfly** has four colourful eyespots that frighten birds. The **cabbage white** lays its eggs on cabbage, and its caterpillars eat the leaves. The **swallowtail** has black and yellow wings with two long tails at the back.

Many butterflies have become rarer. They lack flower meadows and the plants that their caterpillars eat. The caterpillars of the peacock butterfly, for example, live on **stinging nettles**. Anyone who leaves a wild corner with nettles and wild flowers in the garden helps the butterflies. In Switzerland, too, nature conservation organisations campaign for species-rich meadows.

gewusst: The brimstone can live almost a year, which is very long for a butterfly.
Without the scales, butterfly wings would be almost transparent.

teile.einleitung: The blackthorn is a thorny shrub found at woodland edges and in hedges. In spring it is full of white flowers, and in autumn it bears blue-black fruits, the sloes.
wichtigste: The fruits of the blackthorn are called sloes.
Ripe sloes are blue-black with a pale bloom.
The blackthorn blooms in March and April, before the leaves.
Sloes are very sour and tart, and after frost they become milder.
The name blackthorn comes from the dark bark and the thorns.
The sloe is a wild plum and is related to the damson.

abschnitte.text: In March and April the **blackthorn** is full of small **white flowers**. The special thing is that it blooms **before the leaves** grow. That is why the whole shrub then looks as if it were covered with snow. The early flowers are an important food for bees and other insects.

The twigs and the bark of the shrub are very **dark**. It also has sharp **thorns**. That is where the name blackthorn comes from. The shrub spreads by **suckers** from the roots. New shoots grow from them, and in time a dense thicket forms.

The small, round fruits are called **sloes**. When ripe they are **blue-black** with a pale, waxy bloom. Picked early in autumn they taste very **sour** and tart and make your mouth pucker. After the first **frost** they become softer and milder. That is why they are often picked late and made into juice, jelly or jam.

In dense blackthorn hedges, many birds find shelter and room for their nests. The thorns keep enemies away. The **red-backed shrike**, a small songbird, likes to impale its prey on such thorns. The sloe is a **wild plum** and belongs to the **rose family**. It is related to the **damson** and the plum.

gewusst: Sloes often stay hanging on the shrub until winter.
With its suckers, a blackthorn shrub can overgrow whole banks.

teile.einleitung: An urban heat island means that a city is warmer than its surroundings. Especially on summer nights, it cools down much less in the city. With clever planning, this can be eased.
wichtigste: In an urban heat island, the city is warmer than its surroundings.
The difference is greatest on clear, windless nights.
At night it can amount to around 10 degrees.
Concrete and asphalt store a lot of heat.
In the city there is less evaporation and additional waste heat.
On a tropical night, the temperature does not fall below 20 degrees.

abschnitte.text: If you measure the temperature in the city and in the countryside on a summer evening, it is often clearly warmer in the city. On a temperature map, the city lies like a warm island in the cooler surroundings. That is why people speak of an **urban heat island**. It is usually warmest in the **densely built-up centre**.

**Concrete** and **asphalt** store a lot of solar heat during the day. At night they release it slowly again. In addition, densely built-up cities have few plants and little open ground. As a result there is **less evaporation**, which would otherwise cool. On top of that comes **waste heat** from traffic, buildings and **air conditioning**. Narrow streets also hinder the wind.

The difference is greatest on **clear, windless nights**. Then the countryside cools quickly, but the city hardly at all. Between a large city and its surroundings, the difference can be **up to around 10 degrees**. If the temperature does not fall below **20 degrees** at night, it is called a **tropical night**. Such nights are a burden above all on older and sick people, because the body recovers poorly.

In **urban planning** there are many ideas against the heat. **Fresh-air corridors** are open strips through which cool air can flow from the surroundings into the city. **Trees** give shade and cool by evaporation. Green roofs, fountains, pale surfaces and less sealed ground also help. Many Swiss cities are therefore planting more trees and unsealing squares.

gewusst: Pale surfaces reflect more sunlight and warm up less than dark asphalt.
Under a large tree it can feel much cooler on hot days than in the blazing sun.

teile.einleitung: A pest is an animal that damages plants, stored supplies or objects that are important to people. Whether an animal counts as a pest therefore depends on the human point of view.
wichtigste: The Spanish slug is regarded as especially troublesome in Swiss gardens.
The striped Colorado beetle eats potato leaves.
Aphids suck plant sap with a piercing mouthpart.
Their sweet excretion, honeydew, attracts ants.
The box tree moth comes from East Asia and strips box hedges bare.
The spotted wing drosophila lays its eggs in ripe cherries and berries.
The vole eats roots and tubers underground.

abschnitte.text: In nature there are no “good” or “bad” animals. Every animal looks for food. If in doing so it eats vegetables, fruit, forest or stored supplies, people call it a **pest**. Animals that eat pests are called **beneficial insects**, or beneficials, for example ladybirds, hedgehogs or birds. Many pests were brought in from other continents and have hardly any natural enemies here.

The **Spanish slug** is a large, orange to brown slug. It eats lettuce, seedlings and flowers and multiplies rapidly. In Swiss gardens it is regarded as especially troublesome. The **Colorado beetle** has yellow and black striped wing cases. It and its larvae strip the leaves from potato plants. It originally comes from North America.

**Aphids** pierce the plant’s vessels with a **piercing mouthpart** and suck the sugary sap. The sugar they do not need, they excrete as sticky **honeydew**. **Ants** love this sweet juice. They “milk” the aphids and in return protect them from enemies.

The green caterpillars of the **large white**, a white butterfly, eat big holes in cabbage leaves. The **box tree moth** is a moth from **East Asia** that was brought into Europe. Its caterpillars strip whole **box hedges** bare. Many gardens have therefore replaced their box with other shrubs.

The **spotted wing drosophila** is a small fly from **Asia**. Unlike other fruit flies, it lays its eggs in **ripe, healthy fruit** such as cherries, raspberries or grapes. The fruit then goes soft and rots. The **vole** lives underground and eats **roots, tubers and flower bulbs** there. Often you only notice it when a plant suddenly wilts.

gewusst: A ladybird and its larvae can eat thousands of aphids in their lifetime.
The Colorado beetle was so feared in Europe that in the past even school classes were sent out to the fields to collect it.

teile.einleitung: A dough is a soft mass of flour, liquid and other ingredients. It is used to bake bread, plaited loaf, cake or pizza. A lot of interesting things happen in dough while it is kneaded, rested and baked.
wichtigste: A simple bread dough is made of flour, water, salt and yeast.
Kneading makes the dough smooth and elastic.
A yeast dough rises while it rests and becomes about twice as big.
If the dough sticks, a little flour helps.
In Switzerland the dough is rolled out with a rolling pin called a “Wallholz”.
A loaf of bread has a crust on the outside and the crumb on the inside.

abschnitte.text: For a simple loaf, **flour**, **water**, **salt** and **yeast** are enough. No other ingredients are needed. For a plaited loaf, milk, butter and sometimes egg are added. For cakes and biscuits you use sugar and butter. Depending on the ingredients, very different doughs are made.

When you **knead**, the dough becomes smooth and elastic. Flour contains a protein called **gluten**. When kneaded, it forms a stretchy network. Later this network holds the little gas bubbles in place. If the dough sticks too much to your hands, you add a little **flour**, because flour soaks up moisture.

**Yeast** is made of tiny fungi. They feed on sugar from the flour and produce the gas **carbon dioxide**. The gas bubbles puff up the dough, and it becomes about twice as big. That is why a yeast dough is left to rest, covered. A **cloth** keeps it warm and stops its surface from drying out.

For cakes, tarts or pizza, the dough has to be thin. In Switzerland you roll it out with the **“Wallholz”**, which is called **“auswallen”**. In Germany the word for it is “Nudelholz”. A plaited loaf is made by braiding two or more strands of dough. Then the dough goes into the hot oven.

During baking, the surface of the dough becomes hot and dry. That is how the brown, crunchy **crust** forms. Inside, the bread stays soft and airy, and this part is called the **crumb**. In the crumb you can see the holes that formed as the dough rose. The heat in the oven kills the yeast, and the bread keeps its shape.

gewusst: The brown colour of the crust comes from a reaction between sugar and protein in the heat.
In many Swiss families, the “Butterzopf” (butter plait) is a traditional Sunday bread.

teile.einleitung: Summer is the warmest of the four seasons, in Switzerland usually the months of June, July and August. The days are long, the Sun stands high, and nature and people are outdoors a lot. But why is it actually so warm in summer?
wichtigste: In Switzerland, summer is usually the warmest season.
Astronomically it begins around 21 June and ends around 22 or 23 September.
It arises because the Earth’s axis is tilted.
In summer the Sun stands high and shines for a long time.
The longest day of the year is the summer solstice.
In the southern hemisphere it is summer when it is winter with us.
Heatwaves and thunderstorms are typical of summer.

abschnitte.text: The **Earth’s axis** is tilted by about 23.4 degrees. That is why the northern hemisphere faces the Sun for part of the year. The Sun’s rays then strike more steeply and warm the ground more strongly. In addition, the Sun shines for longer, so the air heats up more.

Astronomical summer begins with the **summer solstice** around 21 June. This is the day with the longest daylight, in Zurich about 16 hours. It ends with the equinox around 22 or 23 September. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss count **meteorological summer** more simply from the beginning of June to the end of August.

In summer the temperature on the Central Plateau often rises above 25 degrees, and on **hot days** above 30 degrees. In the afternoon, towering clouds and strong **thunderstorms** often form, sometimes with hail. In the mountains it stays cooler, because the temperature falls by about half a degree for every 100 metres of height. Because of climate change there are more hot days today than 50 years ago.

Plants now grow most strongly, and grain ripens and is harvested in July and August. On the alpine pastures graze cows that moved up to the **Alp** in June. Many birds raise their young, and insects buzz about everywhere. Berries, cherries and apricots ripen.

In Switzerland the **summer holidays** last about five to eight weeks, depending on the canton. People swim in lakes, rivers and open-air pools, or go hiking or to the mountains. On 1 August, Switzerland celebrates its national day with bonfires and fireworks. In the heat it is important to drink a lot, use sun cream and avoid the midday sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the year with typical weather, for example summer or winter.
The day with the longest daylight of the year.
The imaginary line from the North to the South Pole around which the Earth turns.
A day on which it gets at least 30 degrees warm.

gewusst: In summer the Earth is further from the Sun than in winter, and yet it is warmer.
In Australia people celebrate Christmas in summer, often on the beach.
The hottest summer in Switzerland since records began was the summer of 2003.

teile.einleitung: Not every Alpine plant grows everywhere. Whether the soil has formed from limestone or from acidic silicate rock such as granite and gneiss strongly decides which flowers bloom there. People therefore speak of limestone flora and silicate flora.
wichtigste: Limestone soil is basic and has a high pH, silicate soil is mostly acidic.
The hairy alpenrose grows on limestone, the rusty alpenrose on silicate.
Koch’s gentian grows on silicate, the very similar Clusius’s gentian on limestone.
Plants that occur only on limestone are called calcicolous.
When closely related species replace each other on different rock, this is called vicariance.
In Switzerland, limestone flora is found mainly in the Jura and the northern limestone Alps.

abschnitte.text: Soil forms from the rock beneath it. **Limestone** gives a basic soil with a high pH. **Silicate rock** such as granite and gneiss, by contrast, usually gives an acidic soil. The Jura and the limestone ranges on the northern edge of the Alps consist largely of limestone. In the central Alps, for example in parts of the Valais and Graubünden, gneiss and granite predominate.

Some plants have a close relative on the other kind of rock. The **hairy alpenrose** grows on limestone, the **rusty alpenrose** on acidic soil. It is similar with the gentians: Koch’s gentian loves silicate, Clusius’s gentian limestone. This mutual replacement is called **vicariance**, and the species are called vicariant.

On limestone rocks in the Alps the yellow **auricula** blooms. **Edelweiss** also grows mainly on chalky, stony grassland and rock ledges. On limestone typical grasslands thrive, such as blue moor-grass and tufted sedge grassland and cushion sedge grassland. Plants that occur only on limestone are called **calcicolous**.

On acidic silicate, **curved sedge grassland** grows in the alpine zone. Here you also find the pink-flowering hairy primrose on rocks. Bilberry and heather also avoid limestone. Such species are called **calcifuge**.

At a high pH, **iron** in the soil is poorly available. Plants adapted to acidic soils can then hardly take it up. Their leaves turn yellow, which is called **lime-induced chlorosis**. That is why many silicate plants keep away from limestone.

gewusst: Anyone who watches for the alpenrose in the mountains can tell from the shrub whether it stands on limestone or silicate.
This also shows in the garden: blueberries thrive only in acidic soil.

teile.einleitung: In ecology, succession means the step-by-step change of a habitat over time towards a stable state. On bare ground, a few pioneers settle first, then shrubs follow and finally a forest. This sequence can take decades to centuries.
wichtigste: Succession is the natural sequence of communities of living things in one place.
Primary succession begins on completely lifeless ground, for example on rock.
Secondary succession begins after a disturbance, when soil is still present.
Pioneer plants such as lichens and mosses colonise a place first.
At the end there is often a relatively stable state, the climax community.
In Switzerland, succession can be observed well in front of glaciers.

abschnitte.text: The word **succession** comes from Latin and means following on. It means that different communities of living things follow one another in one place. Each group changes the place, for example by forming soil or casting shade. In this way it makes room for the next group of plants and animals.

In **primary succession**, life begins on bare rock, sand or lava, where there is as yet no soil. The first to come are **pioneer plants** such as lichens and mosses. They slowly break down the rock and with their remains form a thin layer of earth. On it, grasses, herbs and finally shrubs and trees can later grow.

In **secondary succession**, a habitat is disturbed but the soil is preserved. This happens, for example, after a forest fire, after a storm such as Lothar in 1999, or when farmers stop mowing a meadow. Here everything is much faster, because seeds and roots are already in the soil. On an abandoned meadow, shrubs grow after a few years and a young forest after a few decades.

At the end of succession there is often a relatively stable state, the **climax community**. On the Swiss Central Plateau this would mostly be a beech forest. In the mountains, spruces, larches or Swiss stone pines often form the final state. Nature never stands completely still, though, because storms, fire or animals keep providing new beginnings.

Because the glaciers in the Alps are melting, more and more bare rock is being exposed. On these **glacier forelands**, for example in front of the Morteratsch Glacier in the Engadine, you can read succession as in a book. Close to the ice only lichens and a few pioneer plants grow. Further away, where the ice lay over a hundred years ago, there are already larches and shrubs.

Many species-rich habitats of Switzerland, such as nutrient-poor meadows and alpine pastures, exist only because people mow or graze them. If the use stops, they slowly become overgrown with bushes and forest, which is called **scrub encroachment**. In Switzerland the forest area is therefore increasing above all in the Alps. Conservationists mow some areas deliberately so that rare plants are preserved.

begriffe.erklaerung: The natural sequence of different communities of living things in one place.
A plant that is the first to colonise a bare place.
The stable end state of a succession, often a forest.
A meadow becoming overgrown with shrubs.

gewusst: After the eruption of Mount St Helens in the USA in 1980, researchers observed how life settled anew on the ash.
Without people, almost the whole of Switzerland below the treeline would be covered in forest.
On the volcanic island of Surtsey off Iceland, which formed in 1963, researchers have studied primary succession from the very beginning.

teile.einleitung: The buddleia is a shrub with long, scented flower spikes. Butterflies love it, which is why it is also called the butterfly bush. In Switzerland, however, it is regarded as a problem plant, because it spreads strongly.
wichtigste: The buddleia originally comes from China.
Its scientific name is Buddleja davidii.
It is not closely related to the true lilac of the genus Syringa.
Its flowers attract many butterflies, but the caterpillars find hardly any food on it.
One shrub can produce up to about 3 million seeds a year.
Gone wild, it often grows on railway land, in gravel pits and on gravel banks.

abschnitte.text: The **buddleia** is native to **China**. It came to Europe as an ornamental shrub and was planted in many gardens. Its scientific name is **Buddleja davidii**, and it belongs to the genus Buddleja. Despite its German name, Sommerflieder, or “summer lilac”, it is not closely related to the true lilac of the genus Syringa. Its long, cone-shaped flower spikes are mostly **violet** to lilac, and garden varieties also come in white or pink.

The scented flowers offer a lot of **nectar**. That is why numerous butterflies often sit on them in summer. This is where the name **butterfly bush** comes from. For native butterflies, though, it helps little. The adult butterflies do drink nectar, but the **caterpillars** of most native species can hardly eat its leaves.

A single shrub produces up to about **3 million** tiny seeds a year. The wind carries them far away, and they stay able to germinate in the soil for a long time. The buddleia loves warm, open and stony places. You therefore find it on **railway land**, in gravel pits and on gravel banks of rivers. There it pushes out native plants. In Switzerland it counts as an **invasive neophyte**, that is, an introduced plant that spreads strongly.

abschnitte.titel: What you can do in the garden
abschnitte.text: Anyone who still has a buddleia in the garden should cut off the faded flower spikes **before the seeds are ripe**. In this way it cannot spread any further. It is even better to replace it with native shrubs. These also offer food for the caterpillars and so really help the butterflies.

gewusst: The buddleia even grows in cracks in walls and on gravel areas with almost no soil.
A garden helps butterflies most when food plants for their caterpillars also grow in it.
